# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L145


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `handler_erc20` smart contract, there is a `support_handler` mapping that checks whether the chain and its handler is supported or not. The problem is that at the moment `receive_cross_chain_callback()` checks whether `to_chain` and `to_handler` are supported on the chain where this function is called. This can lead to incorrect behavior as protocols are supposed to set handler that's supported on the destination chain and not the source chain handler itself.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L144-145
```
            assert(self.support_handler.read((from_chain, from_handler)) && 
                    self.support_handler.read((to_chain, contract_address_to_u256(to_handler))), 'not support handler');
```

As you can see from the logic above, the function verifies if the `to_chain` and `to_handler` is supported on the source chain. The problem is that `support_handler` mapping is created to set destination handler to accept calls from them. But if the function checks whether the `to_chain` is the chain where this function is called, `support_handler` may just not set this handler as supported handler leading to unnecessary DoS. In contrary, here's the corresponding logic on Ethereum:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374-376
```
  if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {
            return false;
        }
```

So it only checks whether `from_handler` from the `from_chain` is supported to make calls to the source chain and the source handler.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Remove the check for `to_chain` and `to_handler`.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L176


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `ChakraSettlement` smart contract, the function `receive_cross_chain_msg()` is called after the message is picked by the validators and signed by them. The function verifies the signatures and the message hash. The problem is that when this tx is sent it can be seen by other people and a malicious user can just front-run the tx and put the same parameters except for payload type. And since `message_hash` is generated without taking into account `payload_type`, the tx will be blocked and its execution set to FAILED as none of the functions will be called in the handler contract.

## Proof of Concept


Take a look at the current implementation of `receive_cross_chain_msg()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-180
```
function receive_cross_chain_msg(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_address,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload,
        uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
        bytes calldata signatures // signature array
    ) external {
```


So it transfers signatures and all the data associated with the message. Now let's look at the way message hash is created:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L183-192
```
  bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    txid,
                    from_chain,
                    from_address,
                    from_handler,
                    to_handler,
                    keccak256(payload)
                )
            );
```

`message_hash` includes all the function parameters except for signatures (that are later verified) and `payload_type`. So a malicious user can just put `ERC721` as a `payload_type` instead of `ERC20` and the transaction will revert:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L316
```
 require(isValidPayloadType(payload_type), "Invalid payload type");
```

So the tx will be set to FAILED (at the moment it just reverts due to another vulnerability but in the future the result will be boolean)

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Include `payload_type` in the `message_hash` or introduce `onlyValidator` modifier.




## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L135
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L118


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `ChakraSettlement` and `ChakraSettlementHandler` contract, there is a `nonce_manager` mapping that's increased every time there is a new cross chain transaction. The problem is that the protocol is supposed to work on zkSync and it may not work due to the problem of nonce ordering.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L118
```
 nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L135
```
nonce_manager[msg.sender] += 1;
```

Nonce is incremented every time `msg.sender` initiates a new cross-chain transaction. But the problem is that the protocol is supposed to work on such chains as zkSync that behave differently from Ethereum. The whole transaction might be reverted due to a ZK overflow. This could lead to a transaction being non-executable forever, which would block future transactions due to nonce ordering without OOO. 

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Create some flag that would point to the out of order execution (depending on the chain). Without nonce ordering enforced, even if a transaction fails due to ZK overflow, which cannot be gracefully handled, it won't block future transactions.


## Assessed type

Other

## Impact

The current version of `ChakraSettlement` smart contract uses `chainId` that's set when initializing the contract.  bytes calldata signatures


These signatures can be potentially reused by other users as anybody can call these functions on the parallel chains due to hard fork happened. Therefore, some undesired scenario may be created when there are too much tokens burnt on the source chain, for example.


## Tools Used

Grok

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Include chainId opcode in the signature schema.

# Vulnerability details

The owner of the handler / settlement contract has to be able to add / remove the owner of the handler. However, on the Starknet chain it cannot be done done so as `remove_handler()` functionality is missing.

## Proof of Concept

There is only `set_support_handler()` function in the cairo version of the handler contract:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L238
```
   fn set_support_handler(ref self:ContractState, chain_name: felt252, handler: u256, support: bool){
            self.ownable.assert_only_owner();
            self.support_handler.write((chain_name, handler), support);
        }
```

According to the spec:

```
Only the owner can add or remove handlers from the whitelist for a given chain.
```

In contrary, this functionality is properly implemented on Ethereum:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L65-70
```
 function remove_handler(
        string memory chain_name,
        uint256 handler
    ) external onlyOwner {
        handler_whitelist[chain_name][handler] = false;
    }

```

Therefore, the current implementation has deviations from the docs resulting in an unexpected behavior where the owner cannot remove the handler in some cases when he needs to.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add `remove_handler()` functionality in the `handler_erc20`.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `ChakraSettlementHandler` smart contract, `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` uses several user-provided parameters that are set as `uint256` instead of bytes / addresses. This is a bad practice as it requires users to encode their address before to the uint256 type creating bad experience / disincentivizing to use the platform.         string memory to_chain,
```
        uint256 to_handler,
        uint256 to_token,
        uint256 to,
        uint256 amount
    ) 
```

If the protocol wants to support non-EVM chains, `bytes` type should be introduced instead of `address`. Otherwise, `address` type has to be used in all other cases.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change `uint256` on `address` type to represent addresses.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L160
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L218


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `ChakraSettlementHandler`, the function `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` serves as an entry point for users to send cross-chain transactions. The problem is that, when creating `CreatedCrossChainTx` for a txId and saving it in `create_cross_chain_txs`, the protocol makes a mistake by storing `address(this)` as `from_token` parameter when in reality it's an address of the `from_handler`

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at the current functionality of `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L268#L154-164
```
 create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
                txid,
                chain,
                to_chain,
                msg.sender,
                to,
                address(this),
                to_token,
                amount,
                CrossChainTxStatus.Pending
            );

```

The struct has `address(this)` parameter on the place where `token` of the handler contract should be:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/BaseSettlementHandler.sol#L59
```
  struct CreatedCrossChainTx {
        uint256 txid;
        string from_chain;
        string to_chain;
        address from;
        uint256 to;
        address from_token;
        uint256 to_token;
        uint256 amount;
        CrossChainTxStatus status;
    }

```

This would result in storing an incorrect information about cross-chain tx and violation of the spec. Moreover, it might potentially affect offchain services as the same mistake is repeated when emitting an event:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L268#L212-222
```
  emit CrossChainLocked(
            txid,
            msg.sender,
            to,
            chain,
            to_chain,
            address(this),
            to_token,
            amount,
            mode
        );
```


## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change `address(this)` parameter on `token` that corresponds to the token of the settlement handler contract.

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L117


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

After cross-chain transaction is initiated inside of `ChakraSettlementHandler`, it goes to the `ChakraSettlement` contract where an event that's monitored by the offchain services is emitted. The problem is that `send_cross_chain_msg()` that's called from the handler contract has no access control at all allowing anybody to manipulate the payload and bypass the information that was submitted by the `ChakraSettlementHandler` smart contract.

## Proof of Concept

As you can see, inside of the function `send_cross_chain_msg`, the handler address is not checked anyhow:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111-120
```
  function send_cross_chain_msg(
        string memory to_chain,
        address from_address,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload
    ) external {
        nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;

        address from_handler = msg.sender;

```

It only takes `msg.sender` and uses it as the `from_handler` address. The function has `external` visibility with no access control modifiers so anybody can just call it and change the payload that was sent from the handler. An attacker can, for example, put all the data that was sent by other users and just slightly change the payload blocking the successful settlement. 


## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

There should be corresponding handler address for the settlement contract initialized in the constructor of the contract that should be checked in all sensitive functions.








## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`TokenRoles` contract is the contract that helps to add / remove operators. The problem is that the contract inherits `UUPSUpgradeable` functionality but does not initialize it in the initialization function not allowing to use upgradeability.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at the current initialization process:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/TokenRoles.sol#L6

```
abstract contract TokenRoles is
    OwnableUpgradeable,
    UUPSUpgradeable,
```

```
    function __TokenRoles_init(address _owner, address _operator) public {
        __Ownable_init(_owner);
        _grantRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, _owner);
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraTokenUpgradeTest.sol#L8
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraTokenUpgradeTest.sol#L25


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`ChakraTokenUpgradeTest` smart contract handles the minting / burning logic by the operator. However, it uses `_authorizeUpgrade()` function (UUPS Proxy) but does not initialize proxy in the `initialize()` function not allowing to use upgradeability in the future.

## Proof of Concept

The contract is supposed to use UUPS upgradeability functionality:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraTokenUpgradeTest.sol#L25-27
```
 function _authorizeUpgrade(
        address newImplementation
    ) internal override onlyOwner {}
```

But the UUPS Proxy is not initialized in the `initialize()` function:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraTokenUpgradeTest.sol#L13-23
```
 function initialize(
        address _owner,
        address _operator,
        string memory _name,
        string memory _symbol,
        uint8 _decimals
    ) public initializer {
        __TokenRoles_init(_owner, _operator);
        __ERC20_init(_name, _symbol);
        set_decimals = _decimals;
    }
```

So it cannot basically use the UUPS upgradeability as it's required to initialize both proxy and `_authorizeUpgrade()`.

Manual review.

Add `__UUPSUpgradeable_init()` in the `initialize()`:

https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/blob/master/contracts/proxy/utils/UUPSUpgradeable.sol#L65-66
```
 function __UUPSUpgradeable_init() internal onlyInitializing {
    }
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L120


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` function serves as an entry for user cross-chain transactions. The problem is that the function does not anyhow validate the `to_handler` address except for address(0) check not checking its validity inside of the source chain handler.

## Proof of Concept

Current validation process looks like this:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L120
```
require(to_handler != 0, "Invalid to handler address");
```

The function does not check validity of the handler on the destination chain even though there is `is_valid_handler()` function inside of the contract:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L41-46
```
 /**
     * @dev Checks if a handler is valid for a given chain
     * @param chain_name The name of the chain
     * @param handler The handler address
     * @return bool True if the handler is valid, false otherwise
     */
    function is_valid_handler(
        string memory chain_name,
        uint256 handler
    ) public view returns (bool) {
        return handler_whitelist[chain_name][handler];
    }

```

So not verifying it on the source chain can lead to DoS on the destination chain and excessive gas costs being spent by the users on the execution.

From the docs:

```
The handler receiving a cross-chain message must be on the whitelist for the source chain
```

Moreover, there is the following check in the Cairo version of the contract:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L168
```
assert(self.support_handler.read((to_chain, to_handler)), 'not support handler');
```


## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add `is_valid_handler` check in the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`.





## Assessed type

Other

title: Incorrect argument order in `CrossChainHandleResult` event emission leads to incorrect cross-chain message finalization
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L238-L241


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When a cross-chain ERC20 transfer is initiated, the destination `ChakraSettlement` contract processes the message via the `receive_cross_chain_msg` function and emits a `CrossChainHandleResult` event. This event is crucial for Chakra validators, as they rely on its arguments to correctly call `ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback` on the source chain to finalize the message.

The issue lies in the incorrect ordering of arguments in the `CrossChainHandleResult` event. This misordering causes the validators to pass incorrect values to the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function, leading to improper message finalization:
```solidity
// cross chain handle result emit by receive side
event CrossChainHandleResult(
    uint256 indexed txid,
    CrossChainMsgStatus status,
    string from_chain,
    string to_chain,
    address from_handler,
    uint256 to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type
);

function receive_cross_chain_msg(
    uint256 txid,
    string memory from_chain,
    uint256 from_address,
    uint256 from_handler,
    address to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type,
    bytes calldata payload,
    uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
    bytes calldata signatures // signature array
) external {
    // --SNIP

    emit CrossChainHandleResult(
        txid,
        status,
>>>        contract_chain_name, // @audit this should be `from_chain`
>>>        from_chain,          // @audit this should be `contract_chain_name`
>>>        address(to_handler), // @audit this should be `from_handler`
>>>        from_handler,        // @audit this should be `to_handler`
        payload_type
    );
}
```

As shown above, the `receive_cross_chain_msg` function incorrectly sets the arguments in the `CrossChainHandleResult` event. When Chakra validators capture this event and use it to call `receive_cross_chain_callback` on the source chain, the wrong values are passed to the function. For instance, the `from_chain` argument in the event emission in `receive_cross_chain_callback` ends up referring to the source chain itself, rather than the intended destination chain that handled the receive message.
## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that the arguments in the `CrossChainHandleResult` event are correctly ordered:
 ```diff
function receive_cross_chain_msg(
    uint256 txid,
    string memory from_chain,
    uint256 from_address,
    uint256 from_handler,
    address to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type,
    bytes calldata payload,
    uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
    bytes calldata signatures // signature array
) external {
    // --SNIP

    emit CrossChainHandleResult(
        txid,
        status,
-       contract_chain_name, 
-       from_chain,          
-       address(to_handler), 
-       from_handler,    
+       from_chain,
+       contract_chain_name,
+       from_handler,
+       address(to_handler)    
       payload_type

    );
}
```


## Assessed type

Other

title: Insufficient Uniqueness in Transaction ID Generation Can Lead to Cross-Chain Transaction Conflicts
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L284-L314


# Vulnerability details

## Description

The `ChakraSettlement` contract is responsible for handling cross-chain transactions. It includes functions to send and receive cross-chain messages, ensuring the integrity and proper processing of these transactions. One critical aspect of this process is the generation of a unique transaction ID (`txid`) for each cross-chain message. The `txid` is generated using the [`send_cross_chain_msg()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L284-L314), which relies on several parameters, including a nonce specific to the sender's address.

The current implementation of [`send_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L284-L314) generates the `txid` as follows:

```js
uint256 txid = uint256(
    keccak256(
        abi.encodePacked(
            contract_chain_name, // from chain
            to_chain,
            from_address, // msg.sender address
            from_handler, // settlement handler address
            to_handler,
            nonce_manager[from_address]
        )
    )
);
```

This approach has two significant issues:
1. The `nonce_manager` is specific to the `from_address`, ensuring uniqueness only per address, not globally.
2. The `txid` generation does not include a unique identifier for the chain, which can lead to collisions if the same `contract_chain_name` is used across different chains.

### Detailed Description

The `send_cross_chain_msg()` function is designed to create a new cross-chain transaction and emit an event with the transaction details. The `txid` is a crucial part of this process, as it uniquely identifies each transaction. However, the current method of generating the `txid` can result in collisions under certain conditions.

Consider the following scenario:
1. User A on Chain X sends a cross-chain message to Chain Y, generating `txid1`.
2. User B on Chain Z (a different chain) sends a cross-chain message to Chain Y, using the same `to_handler` and with the same `nonce_manager` value.
3. If User B happens to have the same address as User A (possible across different chains), and if Chain Z happens to have the same `contract_chain_name` as Chain X, this will generate the exact same `txid1`.

This scenario can lead to:
- Confusion in transaction processing
- Potential overwriting of transaction data
- Exploitation by malicious actors

### Example

1. **User A on Chain X:**
   ```js
   string memory contract_chain_name = "ChainX";
   string memory to_chain = "ChainY";
   address from_address = 0x123...; // User A's address
   address from_handler = 0xabc...; // Handler address
   uint256 to_handler = 0xdef...; // Destination handler
   uint256 nonce = 1; // Nonce for User A

   uint256 txid1 = uint256(
       keccak256(
           abi.encodePacked(
               contract_chain_name,
               to_chain,
               from_address,
               from_handler,
               to_handler,
               nonce
           )
       )
   );
   ```

2. **User B on Chain Z:**
   ```js
   string memory contract_chain_name = "ChainX"; // Same as Chain X
   string memory to_chain = "ChainY";
   address from_address = 0x123...; // Same address as User A
   address from_handler = 0xabc...; // Handler address
   uint256 to_handler = 0xdef...; // Destination handler
   uint256 nonce = 1; // Same nonce as User A

   uint256 txid2 = uint256(
       keccak256(
           abi.encodePacked(
               contract_chain_name,
               to_chain,
               from_address,
               from_handler,
               to_handler,
               nonce
           )
       )
   );
   ```

In this scenario, `txid1` and `txid2` will be identical, leading to a collision.

## Impact
Cross-chain transaction conflicts, incorrect transaction processing, potential loss of funds or unintended token transfers, and compromised integrity of the cross-chain messaging system.

## Proof of Concept
1. User A on Chain X sends a cross-chain message to Chain Y, generating `txid1`.
2. User B on Chain Z (a different chain) sends a cross-chain message to Chain Y, using the same `to_handler` and with the same `nonce_manager` value.
3. If User B has the same address as User A and Chain Z has the same `contract_chain_name` as Chain X, this will generate the exact same `txid1`.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To ensure global uniqueness for each `txid`, introduce a `global_nonce` and include `contract_chain_id` in the `txid` generation.



## Assessed type

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L119-L121


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol smart contract, several require statements are used to verify the validity of certain parameters to ensure they are none zero addresses before proceeding with the function execution. However, the verification checks for to, to_handler, and to_token addresses are improperly conducted as if they were uint256 types rather than address types. This in the best case scenario leads to Dos if an address cannot be verified and worst case loss of fund being transferred to zero address.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L119-L121
The comparisons are made against 0, which is appropriate for uint256 types but not for address types. In Solidity, an address value is considered to be zero if it is equal to address(0) (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000).

Therefore, due to this oversight, the verification won't hold against any transfer made to zero due to ineffective check.
## Tools Used
Manual analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The standard solidity zero address check should be used.
address(0) (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000).



## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

## Impact
This report examines the data types used in the CrossChainLocked event and CreatedCrossChainTx struct in BaseSettlementHandler.sol
 Solidity contract, highlighting the invalid data.
There are critical issues with the usage of uint256 for fields that should be of type address. The fields to and to_token in both the event and struct definitions are incorrectly declared as uint256 when they represent addresses on the destination chain. This creates a scenario where the contract performs in an unexpected manner due to internal errors.

## Proof of Concept
CreatedCrossChainTx:
Invalid. The to field is intended to represent an address on the destination chain. Using uint256 for an address is incorrect and can lead to potential errors.
 Invalid. Similar to the to field, to_token should be of type address to represent a token contract address on the destination chain.
CrossChainLocked:
Invalid. The to field is supposed to represent an address on the destination chain. Using uint256 for this field is incorrect because it does not provide the type safety associated with the address type in Solidity.
Invalid. The to_token field is intended to store an address on the destination chain, similar to from_token. It should be of type address instead of uint256.

## Tools Used
Manual analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change uint256 to to address to in both the event and struct to ensure proper handling of Ethereum addresses.

Change uint256 to_token to address to_token in both the event and struct to maintain type safety and consistency.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The ckrBTC decimals on Starknet is 18 and the ckrBTC decimals on other evm compatible chains is 8. The inconsistent decimals of ckrBTC lead to wrong received amount when bridging between chains with different ckrBTC decimals.

## Proof of Concept
ChakraTokenTest.ts file shows:
```
  const name: string = "ChakraToken";
  const symbol: string = "ckrBTC";
  const decimals = 8;
```
Sponsors also confirm ckrBTC decimals is 8 on evm compatible chains.
The cairo code of ckrBTC uses [openzeppelin erc20 template](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/cairo-contracts/blob/8e660c7b91641afee967a7ed86dd2061d471a861/src/token/erc20/erc20.cairo#L188-L190).
```
        fn decimals(self: @ComponentState<TContractState>) -> u8 {
            18
        }
```
In the openzeppelin erc20 template, the decimals is set to 18.
Let's see what will happen when bridging ckrBTC tokens between chains with different ckrBTC decimals:
Send from Starknet: amount = 1e18, decimals = 18, value = 1 ckrBTC;
Receive on evm compatible chains: amount = 1e18, decimals = 8, value = 1e10 ckrBTC.

## Tools Used
manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the ckrBTC decimals on Starknet to 8.


## Assessed type

ERC20

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L183
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L289
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L138-L165


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If msg_count in handler contract and settlement contract is different, user's message txid is different in handler contract and settlement contract. when `receive_cross_chain_callback` is called, the txid is passed directly from settlement contract to handler contract in receive-callback context. So wrong created_tx key(txid) is used to modify created_tx mapping state and get wrong created_tx mapping state in `receive_cross_chain_callback` function in handler_erc20.cairo.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L183
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L289
There are four handler contracts and one settlement contract on one chain. A user can set cross-chain message by arbitrary handler contract depending on the mode.
The txid is calculated using follow ways:
handler contract →
```
           let tx_id = LegacyHash::hash(get_tx_info().unbox().transaction_hash, self.msg_count.read());
```
settlement contract →
```
            let cross_chain_settlement_id = LegacyHash::hash(get_tx_info().unbox().transaction_hash, self.tx_count.read());
```
The method of calculation is the same in handler contract and settlement contract.
However we have four handler contracts and settlement contract. It's very easy to let msg_count in handler contract and settlement contract not equal as long as more than one handler contracts are used.
For example:
A user send cross-chain message by handler_1 contract. The msg_count/tx_count is same in handler contract and settlement contract. The msg_count/tx_count in settlement contract increments.
And then another user send cross-chain message by handler_2 contract. The msg_count/tx_count is different in handler contract and settlement contract. So the txid in handler contract and settlement contract is different.
Anther case: `send_cross_chain_msg` function in settlement.cairo has no access control, anyone can directly call this function and let tx_count increment. And  then msg_count/tx_count is different in handler contract and settlement contract. So the txid in handler contract and settlement contract is different.
Assume message is received in another chain.
And then `receive_cross_chain_callback` function is called. It pass the txid in settlement contract to handler contract directly. The txid input of `receive_cross_chain_callback` function in handler contract  is from settlement contract. Two txids are different. So wrong created_tx key(txid) is used to modify created_tx mapping state and get wrong created_tx mapping state in `receive_cross_chain_callback` function in handler_erc20.cairo.

## Tools Used
manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Pass the txid in handler contract directly to settlement contract. Keep txid same in handler contract and settlement contract. The txid's calculation includes mode number.





## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L134


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This vulnerability allows a malicious validator to break through the multi-signature verification logic by reusing the same signature into `bytes memory signatures`. Since the contract does not check whether the same validator's signature is used multiple times, the attacker can reuse the same valid signature multiple times, thereby accumulating the number of verification passes (`m`) until the required_validators condition is met.
This signature replay attack will undermine the multi-signature security mechanism of the contract, allowing malicious users to bypass the correct verification logic and perform unauthorized operations, affecting the security of funds and the integrity of the contract.

## Proof of Concept
Link1: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L131-L138

Link2: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L204-L210

### Attack process:
- The attacker only needs to have a valid signature, even if it only meets the signature requirements of one verifier, and they can repeatedly concatenate the same signature into bytes memory signatures.
- Since there is no check for repeated signatures, ++m will be incremented every time the same signature is used repeatedly.
- When the value of `m` accumulates to required_validators , the transaction will be incorrectly considered validated.


**code[For example]:**
```solidity
    // Suppose we have a signatures variable that contains multiple identical signatures
    bytes memory signatures = abi.encodePacked(signature1, signature1, signature1); // Using the same signature three times
```

## Tools Used
- Manual analysis.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To prevent signature replay attacks, it is recommended to add a signature uniqueness check to the contract and ensure that each signature is used only once.

The following measures can be taken:
Track whether each validator's signature has been used through mapping or other data structures to ensure that each signature can only be counted into `m` once.

**Code[For example]:**
```solidity
mapping(address => bool) usedSignatures;

address signer = msgHash.recover(sig);
require(!usedSignatures[signer], "Signature already used");
usedSignatures[signer] = true;
```


## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/AddressCast.sol#L14-L18


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This vulnerability allows incoming bytes32 addresses to not be checked or processed in the expected format. The contract does not verify whether the address is aligned on the left or right end, resulting in potential incorrect address conversion. An attacker may manipulate the contract logic by forging bytes32 addresses, causing invalid addresses to be considered valid, thereby affecting key functions of the contract, such as fund transfer or permission verification.

## Proof of Concept

Link1: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/AddressCast.sol#L14-L18

Link2: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/libraries/AddressCast.sol#L22-L26

This function directly converts bytes32 to address, but does not verify whether the address in bytes32 is aligned on the correct side. Since Solidity addresses are of type uint160 and bytes32 is of type uint256, if the user does not strictly follow the correct alignment, the bytes32 type address conversion will fail if the address is left-aligned, leading to serious security issues.

**Steps to reproduce:**
- If the user's address is: `0x5B38Da6a701c568545dCfcB03FcB875f56beddC4`
- The user encapsulates the address into bytes32 type in the following way:
```solidity
    function convertAddreeToBytes32() external view returns(address) {
        uint160 ms = uint160(msg.sender);
        bytes32 res = bytes32(bytes20(ms));
        return AddressCast.to_address(res);
    }
```
- The output result is: `0x3fCb875F56bEDdc4000000000000000000000000`

From the results, we can see that after the conversion by the `to_address(bytes32 _address)` function, the caller msg.sender and the output result are completely different, which is absolutely not allowed.

## Tools Used
- Manual analysis
- Remix IDE

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent this vulnerability, you need to check whether bytes32 conforms to the valid uint160 address format during address conversion and specify the alignment of the address in bytes32 data. This can be fixed by:

- Verify that the incoming bytes32 data is aligned on the left or right before doing address conversion.

```solidity
    function to_address(
        bytes32 _address
    ) internal pure returns (address result) {
        require(uint256(_address) <= type(uint160).max, "Invalid address format");
        result = address(uint160(uint256(_address)));
    }
```


## Assessed type

Decimal

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Users may lose their funds permanently if an admin removes a handler on the destination chain while a cross-chain transaction is still pending, leading to an incomplete and failed bridging process.

## Proof of Concept

Consider the following Scenario:

1. Alice initiates a cross-chain transaction:

    * Alice wants to bridge 100 Chakra Tokens from Ethereum to BSC using the `BurnUnlock` mode.
    * She calls the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement` function, specifying the destination handler as `X` on the BSC chain from `Y` handler on the Ethereum chain.


2. The transaction remains pending in the Ethereum mempool.

3. While the transaction is pending, the protocol admin decides to remove handler `Y` on the BSC chain by using the `remove_handler` function.

4. When Alice's transaction is finally executed, 100 Chakra tokens are burned on Ethereum as part of the bridging process.

5. Upon receiving the cross-chain message, the BSC chain attempts to process the transfer.

6. Since handler `Y` has been removed from the BSC chain, the following check in `receive_cross_chain_msg` fails at (@->):

```solidity

  function receive_cross_chain_msg(
        uint256 /**txid */,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 /**from_address */,
        uint256 from_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload,
        uint8 /**sign type */,
        bytes calldata /**signaturs */
    ) external onlySettlement returns (bool) {
        //  from_handler need in whitelist
 @->    if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {
            return false;
        }


```
[Link to code](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L311)

7. **Result:** The transaction fails, the status is marked as `CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed`, and Alice's tokens are burned on Ethereum without receiving her 100 Chakra tokens on BSC.

This results in a permanent loss of Alice’s funds with no means to recover them.

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Instead of Checking Validity of Handler in the Destination chain, Check the validity of Handler at the Source chain itself if bridging is possible on that route or not.

This way, if the Chakra team ever needs to remove a handler, the removal will be initiated and checked on the source chain, ensuring no user transactions are processed for a handler that has already been removed.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L334
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L347


# Vulnerability details


## Impact

The bridging process will not correctly handle ERC20 tokens that have different decimals across chains, which can result in significant miscalculations of token amounts.

## Proof of Concept

As per Readme,

> ERC20 used by the protocol:	any

And for chain in which the protocol is going to be deployed on:

> Chains the protocol will be deployed on: Ethereum,Base,Arbitrum,BSC,Optimism,Polygon,zkSync

Some ERC20 tokens have different decimals on different chains. Even some popular ones like USDT and USDC have 6 decimals on Ethereum, and 18 decimals on BSC for example:

- [USDT on Ethereum](https://etherscan.io/token/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7#readContract#F6) - 6 decimals
- [USDC on Ethereum](https://etherscan.io/token/0xa0b86991c6218b36c1d19d4a2e9eb0ce3606eb48#readProxyContract#F11) - 6 decimals
- [USDT on BSC](https://bscscan.com/address/0x55d398326f99059ff775485246999027b3197955#readContract#F6) - 18 decimals
- [USDC on BSC](https://bscscan.com/address/0x8ac76a51cc950d9822d68b83fe1ad97b32cd580d#readProxyContract#F3) - 18 decimals

A more exhaustive list can be found in this [tokens-decimals](https://github.com/magnetto90/tokens-decimals) repository.

**Example Scenario:**

1. Alice wants to bridge 100 USDC from Ethereum to BSC with settlement mode: `LockUnlock`:
    * On Ethereum, USDC has 6 decimals, so Alice’s 100 USDC will be represented as 100e6.

2. Locking USDC on Ethereum:
    * The protocol locks `100e6` USDC on Ethereum as part of the `LockUnlock` settlement mode.

3. Unlocking USDC on BSC:
    * When the cross-chain message is processed on BSC, the protocol attempts to unlock USDC.
    * On BSC, USDC has 18 decimals, so the `100e6` amount is interpreted as `10**-10` USDC on BSC (because BSC expects amounts in 18 decimal format).

This leads to a significant loss of funds for Alice. 

If this process were reversed (bridging USDC from BSC to Ethereum), a small amount locked on BSC could unlock a disproportionately large amount on Ethereum, which could allow someone to drain the entire balance on the Ethereum side.

## Tools Used

VS Code

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Standardize to 18 Decimals on Bridging and then Adjust to Destination Chain Decimals.


## Assessed type

Decimal

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111-L156


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The current method used for generating transaction IDs (`txid`) in the `ChakraSettlement` contract exposes the system to potential front-running and txid manipulation attacks. These vulnerabilities could result in:

Front-running attacks-Malicious actors can observe transactions in the mempool (pending transactions) and submit similar transactions with higher gas prices, ensuring their transactions are processed before the legitimate ones. This can disrupt the transaction order and cause loss of control over cross-chain messages.

`txid` manipulation-Since `txid` is derived from publicly known parameters, attackers could potentially generate conflicting txids, causing issues such as overwriting existing transactions or preventing valid transactions from being processed.

Replay attacks-Without ensuring uniqueness or proper handling of txid, attackers could reuse a valid txid to replay transactions, leading to potential duplicate execution of operations.

## Proof of Concept
In the current `send_cross_chain_msg` function, `txid` is generated as follows:
```solidity
uint256 txid = uint256(
    keccak256(
        abi.encodePacked(
            contract_chain_name, // from chain
            to_chain,
            from_address,        // msg.sender address
            from_handler,        // settlement handler address
            to_handler,
            nonce_manager[from_address]
        )
    )
);
```
This `txid` is deterministic, based on publicly observable parameters such as from_address, to_handler, and nonce_manager. An attacker monitoring pending transactions could replicate these parameters and submit their transaction with a higher gas price to ensure it gets processed first.

Attack Simulation:
An honest user initiates a transaction with the following parameters:
to_chain = "ChainB"
from_address = 0xABC
to_handler = 0xDEF
nonce_manager[from_address] = 1
An attacker observes this transaction and submits the same transaction but with a higher gas fee. The attacker's transaction is mined first, resulting in the same `txid`, causing the original transaction to either fail or be overwritten.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
IncorporatE unpredictable parameters like block.timestamp or blockhash, `the txid` will be harder to predict and manipulate.
```diff
uint256 txid = uint256(
    keccak256(
        abi.encodePacked(
            contract_chain_name,
            to_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            nonce_manager[from_address],
+           block.timestamp,            // Add block timestamp
+           blockhash(block.number - 1)  // Add blockhash for randomness
        )
    )
);
```
This ensures that each `txid` is not only dependent on user inputs but also on the current block's state, making it highly unpredictable.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256-L343


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The lack of proper access control in the `receive_cross_chain_msg` and `receive_cross_chain_callback` functions presents a severe vulnerability. This allows unauthorized parties to call these functions, leading to potential exploitation such as replay attacks where malicious actors resend valid transactions to manipulate the system, griefing attacks where spammed or invalid messages could disrupt the normal operation of the system, potentially freezing or halting cross-chain communication or unauthorized modifications to the state of cross-chain transactions, resulting in financial losses or corruption of data on the destination chain.

## Proof of Concept
The [`receive_cross_chain_msg`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-L244) function can be called by any external party without restriction. Malicious actors can bypass signature verification or even attempt denial-of-service (DoS) attacks by flooding the contract with invalid or repetitive messages, affecting system performance and potentially leading to state corruption.

Similarly, [`the receive_cross_chain_callback`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256-L283) function has no restriction on who can invoke it.
Without access control mechanisms, any attacker could invoke this function to manipulate the status of a cross-chain transaction or disrupt the settlement process.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use access control modifiers such as `onlyAuthorized` or `onlyTrustedRelay` to restrict these functions to be callable only by trusted entities or contracts.



## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111-L133
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-L192
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L139-L150


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Failure to comply with `EIP712` can lead to integration issues and potentially cause a denial of service.

## Proof of Concept
Chakra contract fails to implement the EIP712 in several cases.
According to the [`EIP712 Standard`](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712):

The dynamic values bytes and string are encoded as a keccak256 hash of their contents.
However, in the function `receive_cross_chain()`, the hashing process is handled as follows:
```solidity
function receive_cross_chain_msg(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_address,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload,
        uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
        bytes calldata signatures // signature array
    ) external {
        {
            // verify signature
            bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    txid,
>>                  from_chain,
                    from_address,
                    from_handler,
                    to_handler,
                    keccak256(payload)
                ) 
            );
```
As observed, `from_chain` is `string` value. The hashing (slot) directly encodes this value instead of using the `keccak256` hash of its contents as mandated by the standard.

The same is also observed in `send_cross_chain_msg` function
```solidity
   function send_cross_chain_msg(
        string memory to_chain,
        address from_address,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload
    ) external {
        nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;

        address from_handler = msg.sender;

        uint256 txid = uint256(
            keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
>>                  contract_chain_name, // from chain
>>                  to_chain,
                    from_address, // msg.sender address
                    from_handler, // settlement handler address
                    to_handler,
                    nonce_manager[from_address]
                ) 
            )
        );
```
Here too, `to_chain` and `contract_chain_name` are `string` that are encoded as they are.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Here is the correct implementation; for `receive_cross_chain_msg`
```diff
function receive_cross_chain_msg(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_address,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload,
        uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
        bytes calldata signatures // signature array
    ) external {
        {
            // verify signature
            bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    txid,
-                   from_chain,
+                   keccak256(from_chain),
                    from_address,
                    from_handler,
                    to_handler,
                    keccak256(payload)
                ) 
            );
```
For `send_cross_chain_msg`
```diff
function send_cross_chain_msg(
        string memory to_chain,
        address from_address,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload
    ) external {
        nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;

        address from_handler = msg.sender;

        uint256 txid = uint256(
            keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
-                   contract_chain_name,
-                   to_chain,
+                   keccak256(contract_chain_name), // from chain
+                   keccak256(to_chain),
                    from_address, // msg.sender address
                    from_handler, // settlement handler address
                    to_handler,
                    nonce_manager[from_address]
                ) 
            )
        );
``` 





## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L183-L192


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Consider the following two statements:

1. According to the documentation, the protocol is deployed on multiple chains: Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, BSC, Optimism, Polygon and zkSync. For all these chains except zkSync, the address of the deployed contract depends on the sender's address and nonce. Thus, like many cross-chain DeFi protocols, the address of the `ChakraSettlementHandler` contract could be the same on some of these chains.

2. In `ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg`, the hash on which the signatures are based depends on six factors([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L183-L192)): `txid`, `from_chain`, `from_address`, `from_handler`, `to_handler`, and `keccak256(payload)`. Among these factors, the only one that depends on the target chain is `to_handler`, which is the address of the `handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler` contract. Additionally, while `payload` contains the target chain name, there is no `require` statement to validate this.

Combining the above two issues with the fact that the `ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg` function is `external` and has no access control for calling, a request to mint or unlock tokens for a desired user can be executed across all chains with the same `handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler` contract address.

## Proof of Concept

The hash on which the signatures are based is calculated here:  
([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L183-L192))

```javascript
ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg

    bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
        abi.encodePacked(
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            keccak256(payload)
        )
    );
```

Then, the `to_handler` address is used to call the `ChakraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_msg` function:  
([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L216-L225))

```javascript
ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg

    bool result = ISettlementHandler(to_handler).receive_cross_chain_msg(
        txid,
        from_chain,
        from_address,
        from_handler,
        payload_type,
        payload,
        sign_type,
        signatures
    );
```

In the `receive_cross_chain_msg` function, it only checks the payload validity and extracts `receiverAddress` and `amount` from it. There is no check for target chain validation, and finally, mint or unlock tokens to the target user is executed:  
([code](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L300-L355))

```javascript
ChakraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_msg

    ERC20TransferPayload memory transfer_payload = codec
        .deocde_transfer(msg_payload);

    if (mode == SettlementMode.MintBurn) {
        _erc20_mint(
            AddressCast.to_address(transfer_payload.to),
            transfer_payload.amount
        );
        return true;
    } else if (mode == SettlementMode.LockUnlock) {
        _erc20_unlock(
            AddressCast.to_address(transfer_payload.to),
            transfer_payload.amount
        );

        return true;
    }
```

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this issue, consider adding `chain.id` or `chain_id` to the calculation of the hash to ensure that the signatures are unique to each chain:

```diff
ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg

    bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
        abi.encodePacked(
+           chain.id,
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            keccak256(payload)
        )
    );
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L160


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The 6th parameter in `struct::CreatedCrossChainTx` represents the `from_token` address, as indicated [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/BaseSettlementHandler.sol#L59). However, in `handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement`, when the mapping is set, the 6th parameter is assigned to `address(this)`, which refers to the `ChakraSettlementHandler` contract address instead ([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L160)).

A few lines later, when creating a payload, the 4th parameter of `struct::ERC20TransferPayload` is the `from_token`, and this is correctly set to `AddressCast.to_uint256(token)`, which converts the token address to a `uint256` ([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L185)). This payload is then passed as input to the settlement contract ([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L203)) and is saved with the correct data ([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L142)). Finally, it is emitted ([link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L154)).

According to the document diagram, off-chain Chakra validators retrieve this payload from the network. Since this payload forms part of the hash that is later signed for interaction with the target chain, this vulnerability can lead to discrepancies between the `from_token` saved on the target chain and the initial chain. Additionally, it may cause an invalid signature vulnerability due to the incorrect token address.

## Proof of Concept

The `from_token` address is incorrectly set when creating the `CreatedCrossChainTx` structure in the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement` function:

Definition of `struct CreatedCrossChainTx`:
- [BaseSettlementHandler.sol:59](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/BaseSettlementHandler.sol#L59)
```javascript
    struct CreatedCrossChainTx {
        uint256 txid;
        string from_chain;
        string to_chain;
        address from;
        uint256 to;
        address from_token;
        uint256 to_token;
        uint256 amount;
        CrossChainTxStatus status;
    }
```

Incorrect assignment of `from_token` in `cross_chain_erc20_settlement`:
- [ChakraSettlementHandler.sol:160](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L160)
```javascript
handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement

    create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
        txid,
        chain,
        to_chain,
        msg.sender,
        to,
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L52

# Vulnerability details


**NOTE:** The 4naly3er-report-handler only references the storage gap issue in **Solidity** and not **Cairo** smart contracts.

## Impact

For upgradeable contracts, it is essential to include a storage gap to "allow developers to freely add new state variables in the future without compromising the storage compatibility with existing deployments" (as stated by OpenZeppelin). Without a storage gap, it can be very challenging to write new implementation code. If new variables are added to the base contract without a storage gap, they might overwrite variables in child contracts. This could lead to unintended and serious consequences for the child contracts, potentially resulting in the loss of user funds or causing the contract to malfunction entirely.

Refer to the bottom part of this article:  
[OpenZeppelin Upgrades: Writing Upgradeable Contracts](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/upgrades-plugins/1.x/writing-upgradeable)

## Proof of Concept

Several **Cairo** contracts in the codebase are intended to be upgradeable. However, none of these contracts include a storage gap:

- [Cairo: `handler/src/settlement.cairo`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo)
- [Cairo: `settlement/src/settlement.cairo`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo)


The storage gap is crucial for upgradeable contracts because "it allows us to freely add new state variables in the future without compromising the storage compatibility with existing deployments." Refer to the bottom part of this article:  
[OpenZeppelin Contracts: Upgradeable Storage](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/3.x/upgradeable).

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

It is recommended to add an appropriate storage gap at the end of upgradeable contracts. This practice is common in OpenZeppelin upgradeable contract templates.

**In Cairo:**

Include a storage gap in the `Storage` struct:

```python
struct Storage {
    // other variables...
    _gap: [u8; 50],
}
```

Upgradable

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Some ERC20 tokens have different decimals on the different chains. This means that they need to be handled correctly when they are bridged, otherwise this can cause serious problems like inability to bridge some of the ERC20's or bridge much less tokens to the user. Such example are the USDT AND USDC, they have 6 decimals on Ethereum but 18 decimals on Binance Smart Chain (both of this chains are in the scope of this audit). This problem is present in both the `solidity` and the `cairo` files and the fixes have to be applied in both of the files. For simplicity we will show just the problem in the `solidity` (handler and settlement) files

## Proof of Concept
This POC showcases the bridging of USDC from Ethereum to BSC

Here the user will just send his tokens using the `ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement` that's deployed on the Ethereum chain ( We are just showcasing the settlement mode that just locks on current chain and unlocks the tokens on the destination chain for simplicity)

```
 function cross_chain_erc20_settlement(
        string memory to_chain,
        uint256 to_handler,
        uint256 to_token,
        uint256 to,
        uint256 amount
    ) external {
      
      ...


>>      _erc20_lock(msg.sender, address(this), amount);
        

      ...
```

As we can see we are just sending the amount that the user specified. So if we are bridging 10 USDC the amount will be 10e6 and then this amount is included in the payload and then the message is being sent


```
 function cross_chain_erc20_settlement(
        string memory to_chain,
        uint256 to_handler,
        uint256 to_token,
        uint256 to,
        uint256 amount
    ) external {

    ...

            ERC20TransferPayload memory payload = ERC20TransferPayload(
                ERC20Method.Transfer,
                AddressCast.to_uint256(msg.sender),
                to,
                AddressCast.to_uint256(token),
                to_token,
                amount
            );

            // Create a cross chain msg
            Message memory cross_chain_msg = Message(
                cross_chain_msg_id,
                PayloadType.ERC20,
                codec.encode_transfer(payload)
            );

            // Encode the cross chain msg
            bytes memory cross_chain_msg_bytes = MessageV1Codec.encode(
                cross_chain_msg
            );

            // Send the cross chain msg
            settlement.send_cross_chain_msg(
                to_chain,
                msg.sender,
                to_handler,
                PayloadType.ERC20,
                cross_chain_msg_bytes
            );

    }      
```

Then this payload is emited in the `ChakraSettlement::send_cross_chain_msg()`

```solidity

    function send_cross_chain_msg(
        string memory to_chain,
        address from_address,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload
    ) external {
 
        uint256 txid = uint256(
            keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    contract_chain_name, // from chain
                    to_chain,
                    from_address, // msg.sender address
                    from_handler, // settlement handler address
                    to_handler,
                    nonce_manager[from_address]
                )
            )
        );

       
        create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
            txid,
            contract_chain_name,
            to_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            payload,
            CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending
        );

>>      emit CrossChainMsg(
            txid,
            from_address,
            contract_chain_name,
            to_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            payload_type,
>>          payload
        );
    }


```
Then this payload will be processed by the Chakra Network in the end and  the `ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()` will be called with this payload, and inside the `ChakraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_msg()` will be invoked with it

```solidity

  function receive_cross_chain_msg(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_address,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload,
        uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
        bytes calldata signatures // signature array
    ) external {

       ...

>>     bool result = ISettlementHandler(to_handler).receive_cross_chain_msg(
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            payload_type,
>>          payload,
            sign_type,
            signatures

```

When the tokens are being sent on the Binance Smart Chain here (again we are showcasing just the LockUnlock mode for simplicity)

```solidity

        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 /**from_address */,
        uint256 from_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload,
        uint8 /**sign type */,
        bytes calldata /**signaturs */

       _erc20_unlock(

>>        transfer_payload.amount
```

This will send a super tiny amount because it will send to the user 10e6 USDC instead of 10e18

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a functionality that standardizes the decimals. For example when a user sends his tokens you should write them with 18 decimals in the message (no matter if the token has 18 decimals or not), and then on the destination chain you should also implement a logic that sets the correct decimals of the amount before being sent to the user. Apply this changes in the `cairo` files as well

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
One of the invariants about the Settlement Handler Contract in the README of the audit states that: 

`Cross-chain transaction statuses are properly tracked and updated (Pending, Settled, or Failed).`

The problem is that in the `ChakraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_callback()` this is not handled in the case where the function just returns false because it is coming from an invalid handler. The tx status in `create_cross_txs` remains `Pending` and this breaks the invariant

```solidity

  function receive_cross_chain_callback(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 /* sign_type */, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
        bytes calldata /* signatures */
    ) external onlySettlement returns (bool) {
        //  from_handler need in whitelist
>>       if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {           
>>          return false;
        }

        require(
            create_cross_txs[txid].status == CrossChainTxStatus.Pending,
            "invalid CrossChainTxStatus"
        );

        ...
    }


```

If the `from_handler` is not valid this means that this tx came from invalid handler and the transaction status should be set to `Failed` following the invariant listed by the protocol team

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Set the tx status to Failed when it is coming from invalid handler to follow the invariant

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L327-L385


# Vulnerability details

Note: In this submission, the vulnerability is referred to the Cairo codebase, and this does not apply also for the solidity codebase. 

## Vulnerability details
In the Chakra protocol, the validators call `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg` by signing the `message_hash` in the field `signatures`.

The problem is that differently from the Solidity codebase, in the Cairo codebase, when `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg` is triggered, is not checked if the `txid` has an `Unknown` status or not. Since the status of a transaction is not checked, malicious users could continuously call the function `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg` with the same `txid` and the used signatures of the validators without reverting. 

## Impact
Since people are able to continuously call `settlement:receive_cross_chain_msg`, they are able to mint / unlock tokens from a certain handler, and in this way, they could drain the funds of the entire handler contract. 

## Proof of Concept
When users want to send cross chain transactions, they need to pass through `handler_erc20::cross_chain_erc20_settlement` on the source chain, then, once a event is emitted, the validators will call `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg` on the destination chain using the data of the event and by signing the transaction. 

After the cross chain transaction is completed, the malicious users (those who already sent the previous legit cross chain transaction) could use the same signature of the validator and pass the same arguments to `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg`. In this way they can drain the funds in a certain handler. 

The handler where malicious users could steal funds or mint others tokens is respectively located in the field `to_handler` when calling `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg`. 

Let's make a practical example: 
Let's imagine that Luca (a malicious user) send a legitimate cross chain transaction between `Ethereum` and `Starknet` by locking and unlocking 100 LINK. 

He calls `handler_erc20::cross_chain_erc20_settlement` and locks 100 LINK on `Ethereum`, and then he receives 100 LINK on Starknet when the validators call `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg`. 
Now Luca could start his malicious intention where he could call `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg` on `Starknet` with the same data and signature of the validators (he has it because it has already been used). 
By doing so, every time Luca does this, he will unlock 100 LINK tokens on `Starknet` for free.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
As in `settlement::receive_cross_chain_callback`, make sure that the status of the transaction ids is always checked in `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg`, and allow users to call this function only if the status is set to `Unknown`. 

Consider adding this line of code in `settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg`:

```javascript

assert(self.created_tx.read(cross_chain_msg_id).tx_status ==
CrossChainMsgStatus::UNKOWN, 'tx status error');

```






## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L294


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability description
The `receive_cross_chain_callback` settlement function is intended to only be called by validators, however it is open for everyone but it must assert that the signatures provided match with the message provided in the function:
```
    function receive_cross_chain_callback(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) external {
        verifySignature(
            txid,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        processCrossChainCallback(
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        emitCrossChainResult(txid);
    }
```
Someone can think it is save because even though someone frontruns the transaction and tries to change any parameter it will fail because the message with the parameters has been signed by offchain validators and it must comply that the parameters match. However not all parameters are hashed in the signed message. That is really important because someone can change it and the signatures will still pass.

In this case, the particular parameter that is not signed in the message is the `from_chain` parameter.
```
    function verifySignature(
        uint256 txid,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) internal view {
        bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(txid, from_handler, to_handler, status)
        );

        require(
            signature_verifier.verify(message_hash, signatures, sign_type),
            "Invalid signature"
        );
    }
```

That means that a message that has been signed with the other data can be provided to the function with any arbitrary `from_chain` and it will pass the signature check.

## Proof of concept
1. A user initiates an ERC20 MintBurn type
2. Tokens are minted in the destination chain
3. The validator submits the data in the mempool to call the callback function
4. A malicious user monitors it and frontruns the function call providing the exact same parameters but changing the `from_chain` parameter to any arbitrary string
5. The settlement calls the handler and it returns false because it will not have whitelisted the handler address on this other invented chain string.
```
        if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {
            return false;
        }
```
6. The end result will be the cross transaction marked as failed when it has minted the tokens in the destination chain and the source chain not being able to burn the tokens.
7. The validators call will fail because the cross transaction has a different state of `PENDING`.
```
        require(
            create_cross_txs[txid].status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending,
            "Invalid transaction status"
        );
```



## Impact
The impact of this issue is high because it can be performed by anyone on any message and it prevents executing the logic from the callback function. The current implementation of the callback function in the handler only involves burning tokens but in the future can be more logic that will be skipped. Also the `create_cross_txs` transaction will be marked as failed when in reality the tokens where minted succesfully on the destination chain.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the `from_chain` parameter into the message hashing.
```diff
    function receive_cross_chain_callback(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) external {
        verifySignature(
            txid,
++          from_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        processCrossChainCallback(
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        emitCrossChainResult(txid);
    }

    function verifySignature(
        uint256 txid,
++      string calldata from_chain,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) internal view {
        bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
--          abi.encodePacked(txid, from_handler, to_handler, status)
++          abi.encodePacked(txid, from_chain, from_handler, to_handler, status)
        );

        require(
            signature_verifier.verify(message_hash, signatures, sign_type),
            "Invalid signature"
        );
    }
```



## Assessed type

DoS
