# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374-L376

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An attacker can maliciously modify the cross-chain status through front-running. The successful cross-chain can be modified to be unsuccessful, so [that the contract will not burn the locked tokens](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L383-L393). This affects the functionality of the contract. This is Med.
If the protocol performs manual refunds based on cross-chain status, it is possible to steal the funds in the protocol, which is High. So I judge this finding to be Med/High.

## Proof of Concept
background:
1. In a cross-chain transaction from chain A to chain B, if the protocol is successfully executed on chain B, an event will be emitted, and [chain A will be called from the off-chain to execute the callback](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256).
2. Anyone can call the callback function as long as it has the correct signature.
3. The [from_chain variable is not included in the signature](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L293-L295), so anyone can monitor the memory pool to obtain the signature and use the wrong from_chain to preempt the transaction.
4. [Once from_chain is incorrect, false will be returned in the handler's callback function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374-L376). This bypasses [the _erc20_burn that would be executed normally](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L383-L388).
5. If the protocol performs manual refunds based on the cross-chain status, [using the incorrect from_chain will also mark the cross-chain that should have been Settled as Failed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L317-L331). thereby fraudulently obtaining a refund.

In summary, since from_chain has no signature, the attacker only needs to modify the from_chain and steal the transaction to mark the originally successful cross-chain as Failed. Thereby bypassing _erc20_burn and possible refund fraud.

## Tools Used
manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to include from_chain in the signature as well.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L285-L301


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The `verifySignature` function in the `ChakraSettlement` contract does not properly validate the provided signatures. It constructs a `message_hash` by concatenating the `txid`, `from_handler`, `to_handler`, and `status` values using `abi.encodePacked`. However, it then passes this `message_hash` directly to the `signature_verifier.verify` function without hashing it first.

According to the `ISettlementSignatureVerifier` interface, the `verify` function expects the first argument to be the hash of the message, not the raw message itself. By skipping the hashing step, an attacker can provide signatures that match the raw concatenated message instead of its hash, bypassing the signature verification.

## Impact
This vulnerability allows an attacker to execute unauthorized cross-chain transactions by providing signatures that match the raw concatenated message. The attacker can construct a `message_hash` that satisfies the signature verification without possessing valid signatures from the required validators. 

This can lead to the execution of malicious cross-chain callbacks, potentially resulting in the loss or manipulation of funds and breaking the integrity of the settlement process. Attackers could steal funds, block legitimate transactions, or cause other disruptions.

## Proof of Concept
1. Attacker constructs a malicious cross-chain callback with desired `txid`, `from_handler`, `to_handler`, and `status` values.

2. Attacker calculates the raw concatenated message: 
   ```solidity
   bytes32 message = abi.encodePacked(txid, from_handler, to_handler, status);
   ```

3. Attacker generates signatures that match the raw message instead of its hash, either by signing the raw message directly or finding signatures that coincidentally match.

4. Attacker calls `receive_cross_chain_callback` with the malicious callback data and crafted signatures. 

5. `verifySignature` constructs `message_hash` using `abi.encodePacked` and passes it to `signature_verifier.verify`.

6. Since the signatures match the raw message, the verification succeeds, even though the signatures are invalid for the actual message hash.

7. The malicious callback is processed, bypassing the intended signature verification.

## Tools Used
- Manual code review
- Solidity compiler 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Hash the `message_hash` using `keccak256` before passing it to `signature_verifier.verify`, ensuring signatures are verified against the actual message hash:

```solidity
bytes32 hashed_message = keccak256(message_hash);
require(
    signature_verifier.verify(hashed_message, signatures, sign_type),
    "Invalid signature"
);
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L193-L215


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The `verifyECDSA` function in the `SettlementSignatureVerifier` contract does not properly verify the required number of validator signatures. The function iterates over the `signatures` bytes and verifies each signature individually.

The issue arises in the condition that checks if the recovered signer is a valid validator and increments the counter `m`:

```solidity
if (
    validators[msgHash.recover(sig)] && ++m >= required_validators
) {
    return true;
}
```

This condition returns `true` as soon as the counter `m` reaches the `required_validators` threshold, even if some of the previous signatures were invalid. An attacker can provide a combination of valid and invalid signatures, and as long as there are enough valid signatures to reach the `required_validators` threshold, the function will return `true`.

For example, if `required_validators` is set to 3, an attacker can provide 4 signatures where the first 2 are valid and the last 2 are invalid. The function will return `true` when it reaches the 3rd signature (which is invalid), bypassing the requirement for 3 valid signatures.

## Impact
This vulnerability has severe consequences for the security and integrity of the Chakra settlement process:

1. Unauthorized Transactions: An attacker can execute unauthorized cross-chain transactions by providing a combination of valid and invalid signatures, as long as the number of valid signatures meets the `required_validators` threshold. This bypasses the intended security measures.

2. Reduced Security Threshold: The vulnerability effectively reduces the security threshold of the settlement process. Instead of requiring the prescribed number of valid validator signatures, an attacker can succeed with fewer valid signatures, undermining the distributed trust model.

3. Potential Financial Losses: If exploited, this vulnerability can lead to financial losses for users and the ecosystem. Malicious transactions can result in the theft of funds or manipulation of asset balances.

4. Reputational Damage: The presence of such a vulnerability can damage the reputation of the Chakra protocol and erode trust in its security and reliability.

## Proof of Concept
Here's a step-by-step proof of concept:

1. Assume `required_validators` is set to 3.

2. Attacker prepares a `signatures` bytes array with:
   - Signature 1: Valid signature from a valid validator
   - Signature 2: Valid signature from a valid validator
   - Signature 3: Invalid signature
   - Signature 4: Invalid signature

3. Attacker calls `verifyECDSA` with the prepared `signatures`.

4. Function iterates over signatures:
   - Signature 1: Valid, `m` incremented to 1.
   - Signature 2: Valid, `m` incremented to 2.
   - Signature 3: Invalid, but `++m >= required_validators` becomes true as `m` is incremented to 3, equal to `required_validators`.

5. Function returns `true`, indicating signature verification passed, even though only 2 out of 3 required signatures were valid.

## Tools Used
- Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the `verifyECDSA` function to ensure all required signatures are valid before returning `true`:

```solidity
if (validators[msgHash.recover(sig)]) {
    m++;
    if (m >= required_validators) {
        return true;
    }
}
```

With this modification, the function will only return `true` if all required signatures are valid. If any signature is invalid, the function will continue iterating until all signatures are processed and return `false` if the required number of valid signatures is not met.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The TokenRoles.sol, BaseSettlementHandler.sol, and BaseSettlement.sol contracts are abstract contracts intended for inheritance. However, these contracts lack a storage gap feature. This omission could potentially lead to storage collisions when upgrading contract implementations. In upgradeable contracts, this issue could result in unintended overwriting of variables in child contracts by new variables added to the base contract during upgrades.

## Proof of Concept
You can check the following link as a reference from OZ:
https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/3.x/upgradeable#:~:text=Storage%20Gaps,50%20storage%20slots).

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add storage gaps to the abstract contracts. Consider using the following pattern:
```
uint256[50] private __gap;
```
This pattern aligns with best practices recommended by OZ for upgradeable contract deployments. By implementing this storage gap, developers can safely extend contract functionality without risking unintended consequences in existing deployments.


## Assessed type

Upgradable

# Lines of code

 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L183-L190


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Attacker will be able to steal funds on other evm chains by reusing signature that was meant for a particular EVM chain

## Proof of Concept

When calling receive_cross_chain_msg on a dest chain, caller must supply a "signatures" field.

This signature is expected to be from validators, and the message signed includes: [txid, from_chain, from_address, from_handler, to_handler, keccak256(payload)].

The issue is, the signed message does not include the to_chain_id. This allows reuse of the same signature across multiple EVM chains:
```solidity
    function receive_cross_chain_msg(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
```

The above logic applies for BurnUnlock type.

Since tokens are not refundable on source chain, Alice(and other competitors) has to hope for someone else to make a matching CCTX(which has a very low chance of happening)

# Vulnerability details

In the `receive_cross_chain_msg` function, the `CrossChainHandleResult` event emits `from_chain(source chain) `as `contract_chain_name` and `to_chain(destination chain)` as `from_chain`. However, the `contract_chain_name` should represent the destination chain, while the rest should represent the source chain. This will allow validators to correctly callback via the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function and finalize the user's message.

```solidity
 event CrossChainHandleResult(
        uint256 indexed txid,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        string from_chain,
        string to_chain,
        address from_handler,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type
    );
```

```solidity
emit CrossChainHandleResult(
            txid,
            status,
            contract_chain_name,
            from_chain,
            address(to_handler),
            from_handler,
            payload_type
        );
```

## Impact
Validators might burn tokens on the wrong chain when the mode is `MintBurn`.
```solidity
if (status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Success) {
            if (mode == SettlementMode.MintBurn) {
                _erc20_burn(address(this), create_cross_txs[txid].amount); 
            }

            create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainTxStatus.Settled;
        }
```

Validators maybe not be able to verify and finalize transactions.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L235C1-L244C6

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider replacing `contract_chain_name` with `from_chain`.

```diff
emit CrossChainHandleResult(
            txid,
            status,
+           from_chain, // Source chain
+           contract_chain_name, // Destination chain
            address(to_handler),
            from_handler,
            payload_type
        );
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/utils.cairo#L429
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/utils.cairo#L446


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Array slicing is done wrongly causing unintended values to end up in sliced array or possible out of bounds error.

## Proof of Concept
The u128_array_slice and u64_array_slice functions are intended to return a slice (sub-array) of an input array src of u128 and u64 elements, starting from a specified begin index and ending at a specified end index. However, the current implementation wrongly calculates where the slicing is meant to end leading to a wrong slicing of the array. 

```
let len = begin + end;
```
The len variable above used to determine the number of iterations of elements to be slices is calculated by adding the specified begin and end inputs. Which shouldnt be so, as in standard array slicing, the end represents the index at which the slicing stops. Therefore adding it to the begin index and using the sum as the point to stop the slicing will cause it return fewer or more elements than intended, or even fail to slice the array correctly due to an out of bounds error.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Calculate the len as follows:
```
if end > src.len() {
    let len = src.len();
}else {
    let len = end;
}
```



## Assessed type

Loop

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111-L150


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The current implementation of cross-chain transaction ID generation in the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement` function lacks a unique identifier for the source chain. This omission creates a vulnerability where an attacker could potentially replay a transaction on another chain if the same user address, handler addresses, and nonce exist on both chains. Such a replay attack could lead to unauthorized token transfers, double-spending, or other malicious activities, resulting in financial losses.

## Proof of Concept
In the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement` function, the transaction ID (txid) is generated as follows:

```solidity
uint256 txid = uint256(
    keccak256(
        abi.encodePacked(
            chain,
            to_chain,
            msg.sender,
            address(this),
            to_handler,
            nonce_manager[msg.sender]
        )
    )
);
```

This implementation does not include a unique identifier for the source chain, such as a chain ID or a network-specific constant. As a result, if the same user address, handler addresses, and nonce exist on two different chains, it's possible to generate the same txid, potentially allowing a transaction to be replayed on another chain.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Include a unique chain identifier in the txid generation. This could be chain ID.



## Assessed type

ERC20

title: Missing from_chain parameter in message_hash allows attacker to block callbacks
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256


# Vulnerability details

## Summary

**Context:**
Here is the execution path when a cross-chain ERC20 transfer call occurs:

Source chain:
[cross_chain_erc20_settlement()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111) => [send_cross_chain_msg()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111)

Destination chain:
[receive_cross_chain_msg()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170) => [receive_cross_chain_msg()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L300)

Source chain:
[receive_cross_chain_callback()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256) => [receive_cross_chain_callback()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L365)

**Issue:**
The issue in this execution path lies in the receive_cross_chain_callback() call on the source chain. When the signature verification occurs [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L265C8-L272C11), it does not include the `from_chain` parameter (i.e. the destination chain) for the message verification.

**Impact:**
Due to this, an attacker could frontrun the relayer's [receive_cross_chain_callback()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256) call with the same call. The only difference would be that the attacker supplies the `from_chain` parameter as a random uint256.

Since the `from_chain` parameter was not validated by the signature and is now a random value, the call to the [receive_cross_chain_callback()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374C8-L376C10) function on the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol contract would return false due to check [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374C8-L376C10). This would set the tx status to FAILED on the ChakraSettlement.sol contract [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L329) even though the call had succeeded on the destination chain. 


The impact of this is that successful MINT_BURN mode calls would not have their tokens burnt on the source chain and would remain locked in the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol contract (see [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L383C9-L389C10)). 

## Proof of Concept

Let's go through the issue step by step:

1. We assume an ERC20 cross-chain call occurs from chain A to chain B. The call succeeds on chain B. The settlement mode is MINT_BURN.

2. The relayer calls the receive_cross_chain_callback() function on the ChakraSettlement.sol contract. The attacker sees this incoming call in the mempool and frontruns it with the exact same parameters except for the `from_chain` parameter, which would be some invalid chain not supported by the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol contract.
 - First, the verifySignature() function is called. As we can see from the parameters passed, it does not even use the `from_chain` parameter anyway. We'll see this in step 3.
 - Second, the processCrossChainCallback() function is called. We'll see this in  step 4.
```solidity
File: ChakraSettlement.sol
264:     function receive_cross_chain_callback(
265:         uint256 txid,
266:         string memory from_chain,
267:         uint256 from_handler,
268:         address to_handler,
269:         CrossChainMsgStatus status,
270:         uint8 sign_type,
271:         bytes calldata signatures
272:     ) external {
273:         verifySignature(
274:             txid,
275:             from_handler,
276:             to_handler,
277:             status,
278:             sign_type,
279:             signatures
280:         );
281:         processCrossChainCallback(
282:             txid,
283:             from_chain,
284:             from_handler,
285:             to_handler,
286:             status,
287:             sign_type,
288:             signatures
289:         );
290:         ...
291:     }
```

3. In the verifySignature() function, we can see that the `message_hash` does not include the `from_chain` parameter, which means it is not validated by the signatures of the validators.

```solidity
File: ChakraSettlement.sol
293:     function verifySignature(
294:         uint256 txid,
295:         uint256 from_handler,
296:         address to_handler,
297:         CrossChainMsgStatus status,
298:         uint8 sign_type,
299:         bytes calldata signatures
300:     ) internal view {
301:        
302:         bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
303:             abi.encodePacked(txid, from_handler, to_handler, status)
304:         );
305: 
306:         require(
307:             signature_verifier.verify(message_hash, signatures, sign_type),
308:             "Invalid signature"
309:         );
310:     }
```

4. The processCrossChainCallback() function does the following:
 - Checks if the status of txid is PENDING (meaning the call was sent from source but has not received a callback)
 - Makes a call to the processCrossChainCallback() function on the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol contract.
 - If the call returns true, it sets the status of the transaction to the `CrossChainMsgStatus status` parameter (which represents that the call validly failed or succeeded on the destination chain).
 - If the call returns false, it simply treats the callback as invalid and sets the status to FAILED. 

```solidity
File: ChakraSettlement.sol
312:     function processCrossChainCallback(
313:         uint256 txid,
314:         string memory from_chain,
315:         uint256 from_handler,
316:         address to_handler,
317:         CrossChainMsgStatus status,
318:         uint8 sign_type,
319:         bytes calldata signatures
320:     ) internal {
321:         require(
322:             create_cross_txs[txid].status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending,
323:             "Invalid transaction status"
324:         );
325: 
326:         if (
327:             ISettlementHandler(to_handler).receive_cross_chain_callback(
328:                 txid,
329:                 from_chain,
330:                 from_handler,
331:                 status,
332:                 sign_type,
333:                 signatures
334:             )
335:         ) {
336:           
338:             create_cross_txs[txid].status = status;
339:         } else {
340:           
341:             create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed;
342:         }
343:     }
```

5. The receive_cross_chain_callback() call to the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol contract would return false. This is because although the `from_handler` was validated by the signature verification in step 3, the `from_chain` is invalid. Due to this, Line 388 returns false to the processCrossChainCallback() function and marks it as FAILED even if the call on the destination succeeded i.e. `CrossChainMsgStatus status` = CrossChainMsgStatus.Success. 
 - Due to this, if the MINT_BURN call had succeeded on the destination chain (see Line 397), the tokens that were transferred to the contract by the user in step 1 are not burnt and remain in the contract locked. Additionally, the status remains PENDING and does not transition in ChakraSettlementHandler.sol even though it is marked FAILED in the ChakraSettlement.sol contract.
```solidity
File: ChakraSettlementHandler.sol
376:      */
377:     function receive_cross_chain_callback(
378:         uint256 txid,
379:         string memory from_chain,
380:         uint256 from_handler,
381:         CrossChainMsgStatus status,
382:         uint8 /* sign_type */, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
383:         bytes calldata /* signatures */
384:     ) external onlySettlement returns (bool) {
385:         //  from_handler need in whitelist
386:         
387:         if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {
388:             return false;
389:         }
390: 
391:         require(
392:             create_cross_txs[txid].status == CrossChainTxStatus.Pending,
393:             "invalid CrossChainTxStatus"
394:         );
395: 
396:         
397:         if (status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Success) {
398:             if (mode == SettlementMode.MintBurn) {
399:                 _erc20_burn(address(this), create_cross_txs[txid].amount);
400:             }
401: 
402:             create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainTxStatus.Settled;
403:         }
404: 
405:        
406:         if (status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed) {
407:             create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainTxStatus.Failed;
408:         }
409: 
410:        
411:         return true;
412:     }
```

6. The callback cannot be retried from the ChakraSettlement.sol contract since the status is set to FAILED permanently. 

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Include the `from_chain` in the message_hash when validating signatures.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

**Context:**

Here is the execution path when a cross-chain ERC20 transfer call occurs:

Source chain:
[cross_chain_erc20_settlement()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111) => [send_cross_chain_msg()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111)

Source chain:
[receive_cross_chain_callback()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256) => [receive_cross_chain_callback()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L365)

**Issue:**
The issue exists in [receive_cross_chain_callback()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L365) function in the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol contract. If a call fails on the destination chain (in case the `from_handler` and `from_chain` is removed as a valid handler on the destination chain before the user's transaction takes place), the tokens locked/burned on the source chain are not minted back to the user. 

**Impact:**
Due to this, since a FAILED message is not retriable on the source chain, the tokens on the user are permanently locked in the ChakraSettlementHandler.sol contract on the source chain.

## Proof of Concept

1. User calls cross_chain_erc20_settlement on the source chain handler contract, which calls the send_cross_chain_msg() function on the ChakraSettlement.sol contract.

2. Let's say the `from_chain` and `from_handler` are removed on the destination chain.

3. When the receive_cross_chain_msg() function is called on the destination chain, it checks if the source sending the message is a valid handler. Since it is not, it returns false to receive_cross_chain_msg() on the ChakraSettlement.sol contract and marks the transaction as FAILED.

```solidity
File: ChakraSettlementHandler.sol
305:     function receive_cross_chain_msg(
306:         uint256 /**txid */,
307:         string memory from_chain,
308:         uint256 /**from_address */,
309:         uint256 from_handler,

311:         bytes calldata payload,
312:         uint8 /**sign type */,
313:         bytes calldata /**signaturs */
314:     ) external onlySettlement returns (bool) {
315:         //  from_handler need in whitelist
316:         if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {
317:             return false;
318:         }
```

4. When the receive_cross_chain_callback() call arrives on the source chain from the destination chain, on line 407 the status is marked as FAILED but the locked/burned tokens are not refunded to the user.

```solidity
File: ChakraSettlementHandler.sol
377:     function receive_cross_chain_callback(
378:         uint256 txid,
379:         string memory from_chain,
380:         uint256 from_handler,
381:         CrossChainMsgStatus status,
382:         uint8 /* sign_type */, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
383:         bytes calldata /* signatures */
384:     ) external onlySettlement returns (bool) {
385:         //  from_handler need in whitelist
386:      
387:         if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {
388:             return false;
389:         }
390: 
391:         require(
392:             create_cross_txs[txid].status == CrossChainTxStatus.Pending,
393:             "invalid CrossChainTxStatus"
394:         );
395: 
397:         if (status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Success) {
398:             if (mode == SettlementMode.MintBurn) {
399:                 _erc20_burn(address(this), create_cross_txs[txid].amount);
400:             }
401: 
402:             create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainTxStatus.Settled;
403:         }
404: 
405:      
406:         if (status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed) {
407:             create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainTxStatus.Failed;
408:         }
409: 
410:          
411:         return true;
412:     }
```

5. Due to this, the tokens of the user are permanently locked in the handler contract.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider allowing users to retrieve their source chain tokens when calls on the destination chain fails. This can be done by the checking for the FAILED status set by the callback on the source chain.


## Assessed type

DoS

raw_row.title: Truncation Issue When Casting `bytes32` to `address` in `to_address` Function

title: Truncation Issue When Casting `bytes32` to `address` in `to_address` Function
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/AddressCast.sol#L17


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `to_address` function in the `AddressCast.sol` library casts a `bytes32` value to an `address` by first converting it to `uint256` and then truncating it to `uint160`. This truncation discards the most significant 96 bits of the `bytes32` value. If the input `bytes32` value contains non-zero data in the most significant 96 bits, that data will be lost, leading to an incorrect `address` being returned.

This issue can result in incorrect behavior if the input `bytes32` value is not properly validated. Specifically, if the input is expected to represent an `address`, the most significant 96 bits should always be zero. However, if the input is arbitrary or comes from an untrusted source, there is a risk that the truncation could lead to an invalid or unintended `address`.

## Proof of Concept
The issue occurs in the following function in the `AddressCast.sol` file:

```solidity
function to_address(
    bytes32 _address
) internal pure returns (address result) {
    result = address(uint160(uint256(_address)));
}
```

### Example of Truncation:
If the input `_address` is the following `bytes32` value:

```
0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF000000000000000000000000
```

- The most significant 96 bits (`0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`) will be discarded when casting to `uint160`.
- The resulting `address` will be:

```
0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
```

This is not the intended behavior, as the original `bytes32` value contained non-zero data in the most significant bits.

### Code Reference:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/AddressCast.sol#L17

## Tools Used
- Manual code review
- Solidity documentation - https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/types.html

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent this truncation issue, add a validation check to ensure that the most significant 96 bits of the `bytes32` value are zero before performing the cast. Here's the recommended fix:

```solidity
function to_address(
    bytes32 _address
) internal pure returns (address result) {
    // Ensure that the most significant 96 bits are zero
    if (uint256(_address) >> 160 != 0) {
        revert AddressCast_InvalidAddress();
    }
    result = address(uint160(uint256(_address)));
}
```

This check ensures that the input `bytes32` value is within the valid range for an `address`, preventing unintended truncation of important data.


## Assessed type

Under/Overflow

raw_row.title: Truncation Vulnerability in `MessageV1Codec.sol` Due to Incorrect `id` Type Casting

title: Truncation Vulnerability in `MessageV1Codec.sol` Due to Incorrect `id` Type Casting
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/MessageV1Codec.sol#L56-L58


# Vulnerability details

## **Impact**

The struct `Message` in `Message.sol` contains `id` which was defined as a `uint256`, but in the contract `MessageV1Codec.sol`, the function `id` is extracted from `_msg[1:33]` which contains 32 bytes and was cast to `byte8` which was further cast to `uint64`. This results in **truncation** of the `id`, where only the lower 64 bits of the value are retained, and the higher 192 bits are discarded. This truncation can lead to:

1. **Loss of Data**: The full `uint256` `id` is not preserved, which can cause incorrect behavior if the `id` is used for critical operations.
   
2. **Collision Risk**: Different `uint256` values could map to the same `uint64` value, leading to **id collisions**. An attacker could exploit this to manipulate the contract's behavior, especially if the `id` is used for transaction identification, cross-chain message handling, or access control.

3. **Incorrect Logic**: If the contract logic relies on the full `uint256` `id` for uniqueness or correctness, truncating it to `uint64` could lead to incorrect behavior, such as misidentifying transactions or allowing unauthorized access.


### **Proof of Concept**

#### Code Reference:

- **`Message.sol`**: The `id` is defined as a `uint256` in the `Message` struct.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/Message.sol#L32-L39

  ```solidity
  struct Message {
      uint256 id;
      PayloadType payload_type;
      bytes payload;
  }
  ```

- **`MessageV1Codec.sol`**: The `id` function incorrectly extracts only 8 bytes and casts it to `uint64`.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/MessageV1Codec.sol#L56-L58

  ```solidity
  function id(bytes calldata _msg) internal pure returns (uint64) {
      return uint64(bytes8(_msg[ID_OFFSET:PAYLOAD_TYPE_OFFSET]));
  }
  ```

#### Vulnerability Demonstration:

1. **Truncation Example**:
   - If the `id` is a `uint256` with the value:
     ```solidity
     uint256 id = 0x1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef;
     ```
   - The current code in `MessageV1Codec.sol` will extract only the first 8 bytes and cast it to `uint64`:
     ```solidity
     uint64 truncatedId = uint64(bytes8(_msg[ID_OFFSET:PAYLOAD_TYPE_OFFSET]));
     ```
   - This results in the truncated value:
     ```solidity
     truncatedId = 0x1234567890abcdef;
     ```
   - The higher-order bytes (`0x1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef`) are lost, and only the lower 64 bits (`0x1234567890abcdef`) are retained.

2. **Collision Example**:
   
Two different `bytes calldata _msg` can be give exactly the same id


### **Tools Used**

- Manual code review

### **Recommended Mitigation Steps**

1. **Update the `id` function in `MessageV1Codec.sol`** to extract the full 32 bytes and cast it to `uint256`, rather than truncating it to `uint64`. Here's the updated code:

   ```solidity
   function id(bytes calldata _msg) internal pure returns (uint256) {
       require(_msg.length >= PAYLOAD_TYPE_OFFSET, "Message too short");
       return uint256(bytes32(_msg[ID_OFFSET:PAYLOAD_TYPE_OFFSET]));
   }
   ```

2. **Ensure consistency** between the `id` type in `Message.sol` and `MessageV1Codec.sol`. If the `id` is defined as `uint256` in `Message.sol`, it should be handled as `uint256` throughout the codebase.

## Impact
In the AddressCast contract the toAddress() will change the type of an input from bytes32 and uint256 to an address:
uint256 -> address
bytes32 -> address

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/libraries/AddressCast.sol#L14-L24

and when the off-chain actors forward the message, and let the target on-chain contract to validate the message, this can bring up a risk of address truncating, because the toAddress() function that being used will truncate the uint256 and bytes32 address to the correct address format.

for example other chain initiate a message that will interacting this address.

0x000000000000000000C02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2 (WETH)
after toAddress() this WETH address will become 
0xC02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2 (WETH)


However, this address 
0xAA0000000000000000C02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2 (malicious WETH)
through toAddress() will also resolve to valid WETH address
0xC02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2 (WETH)

```
uint256 public wethAddress = uint256(uint160(address(0xC02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2)));

function to_address( uint256 _address) external view returns (address result) {
	result = address(uint160(_address));
}
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the contest readme under the trusted role section it says nothing about validators being trusted so we can and should assume the worst.
Rogue validators can replay a message multiple times hence draining user's funds stored on the contract.

## Proof of Concept
Validators are in charge of processing messages on destination chains which can typically be anybody that is assigned to do this so it makes sense they can become malicious adding to the major fact that contest readme does not dispute this. The processing is done by collecting the signatures of required number of validators to process the cross chain message
 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L350
 The issue here is that in `settlement.cairo`, the function `receive_cross_chain_msg()` does not check if the state of the message is already sucessful. It just writes the state to either `successful` or `failed` and that is all. So a rogue or malicious validator can send 10 ether on let's say ethereum come to starknet and replay that message payload 100 times getting 1000 ether; much info was not given on how the collection of required validators signatures will be done but this malicious validator will behave as if they want to sign a normal transaction so it will go through. Adding to this another completely honest validator might actually pick an already processed message payload up and it will be a successful transaction giving the `to` double of their tokens or more. Relevant codelink is posted above 


## Tools Used
Manual Review 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add an assert message to ensure the message state is not successful before the operation is done

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L130-L140
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L203-L213


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If a single validator is compromised, it could sign a message that would cause `ChakraSettlementHandler` to unlock a large number of locked assets and send them to an attacker's address.

The purpose of having `SettlementSignatureVerifier.required_validators` is to provide a level of protection against a single validator being compromised. If that were to happen, it would not be desirable for the entire protocol to be compromised. Similarly, once the TVL of Chakra becomes significant, the incentive for a single validator to sign a bad message could become significant, allowing themselves to potentially steal large amounts of locked assets.

If any single validator can unilaterally sign messages, the entire Chakra protocol becomes as strong as its weakest validator.

## Proof of Concept
When `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_msg()` receives a cross chain message, it calls `signature_verifier.verify()` to validate the signatures. The logic for this validation is contained in  `SettlementSignatureVerifier.verifyECDSA()`. This function contains a loop which steps through the `signatures` byte array in steps of 65 characters (a signature's length) and checks each one to see if it is a valid signature of a validator. This is done by calling Openzeppelin's `ECDSA.recover()` on the individual signature and then looking up the returned signer address in the mapping `validators`.

However, there is nothing in this logic to prevent the `signatures` `bytes` array from consisting of the same single signature repeated multiple times. This would repeatedly pass the test on lines 207/134:
```
validators[msgHash.recover(sig)] && ++m >= required_validators
```
This would increase the variable `m` as many times as the signature is repeated, and so allow a single signature to count as enough to satisfy the condition of needing `required_validators` signatures to validate a received cross chain message, regardless of the value of `required_validators`.

## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
As well as incrementing  the `uint256 m` inside `verifyECDSA()`, create an empty `address[]` array of length `required_validators`. When a signature is confirmed as coming from a known validator, check for the validator's address in this array and, if it is not found, add it. It may be useful to make use of a library that implements unique arrays with lookup functions.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

The purpose of having the storage variable `required_validators_num` in the `ChakraSettlement` contracts is to provide a level of protection against a single validator being compromised. If that were to happen, it would not be desirable for the entire protocol to be compromised. Similarly, once the TVL of Chakra becomes significant, the incentive for a single validator to sign a bad message could become significant, allowing themselves to potentially steal large amounts of locked assets.

If any single validator can unilaterally sign messages, the entire Chakra protocol becomes as strong as its weakest validator.

This is done by calling `core::ecdsa::recover_public_key()` on the individual signature and then looking up the returned public key in the `LegacyMap` `chakra_validators_pubkey`. If it is found, then the variable `pass_count` is incremented.

```
let pub_key: felt252 = recover_public_key(message_hash,r,s,y).unwrap();
if self.chakra_validators_pubkey.read(pub_key) > 0{
```

Manual inspection

As well as incrementing `pass_count` inside `check_chakra_signatures()`, create an empty `seen_pubkeys` array. When a signature is confirmed as coming from a known validator, check for the validator's address in this array and, if it is not found, add it. It may be useful to make use of a library that implements unique arrays with lookup functions.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L198-L203
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L197-L202
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L173-L190
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L174-L191


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Although the likelihood of a manager setting the number of required validators to zero is low, the impact would be extreme: it would allow any user to successfully submit any cross chain message to the protocol.

This would essentially unlock all tokens held by the relevant handler contract to any user, and also allow any other handlers to be compromised.

## Proof of Concept
The functions `set_required_validators_num()` have no checks on the value of the argument `new_num`. It can be zero.

If `required_validators_num` is zero, any non-empty array of signatures will be approved by `self.check_chakra_signatures()`. A public key returned by `core::ecdsa::recover_public_key()` does not need to be a registered validator; it simply needs to not revert and so the signature checking loop can break:
```
if i > signatures.len()-1{
    break;
}
```
And then the `assert` test at the end of the function will always pass if `required_validators_num` is zero:
```
assert(pass_count >= self.required_validators_num.read(), 'Not enough validate signatures');
```

And so any cross chain message is now valid and the protocol on Starknet has effectively no signature protection.

Note that this vulnerability does not exist in the Solidity code because, to return true, `verifyECDSA()` will always need at least one valid signature from a validator because of the short circuit effect of the `&&` operator in this test:
```
if (
validators[msgHash.recover(sig)] && ++m >= required_validators
) {
return true;
}
```

## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a requirement in `set_required_validators_num` that `new_num` be greater than zero. 


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L325-L383
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L327-L385
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L108-L136


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Tokens can be stolen from the protocol by any user because of this vulnerability. A valid cross chain message sent to Starknet which mints or unlocks tokens can be replayed an unlimited number of times, thus allowing an attacker to potentially empty the handler contract of all assets or mint an unlimited number of Chakra bridged ERC20 tokens.

Other handlers that rely on `ChakraSettlement` to only call them once per `cross_chain_msg_id` would also be exploitable.

Also, as the events are emitted multiple times, it is possible that off chain systems and bridges that monitor this event could also be exploited.

## Proof of Concept
The functions `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_msg()` do not perform a check on the existing status of `self.received_tx` for the received `cross_chain_msg_id`.

The functions verify signatures, but then go on to call handlers and emit the event and return `true`. It would therefore be possible for any address to resubmit a valid received cross chain message and have it processed multiple times.

Within `ERC20HandlerImpl`, its function `receive_cross_chain_msg` would be called by the `settlement` contract on this line:
```
let success = handler.receive_cross_chain_msg(cross_chain_msg_id, from_chain, to_chain, from_handler, to_handler , payload);
```
The code of `ERC20HandlerImpl.receive_cross_chain_msg()` validates its input by testing to see if the settlement and handler contracts are valid. It does not check that the `cross_chain_msg_id` has not been seen before, and will therefore proceed to mint/transfer tokens repeatedly for the same message.

## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_msg()` perform a check on the existing status of `self.received_tx` for the received `cross_chain_msg_id` and do not process the message if it has already been received.

It may also be recommended to check `cross_chain_msg_id` in `ERC20Handler.receive_cross_chain_msg()` and any other handlers, although this is an additional layer of security and should not be necessary if `ChakraSettlement` is performing the check.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-L244
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L300-L355


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Tokens can be stolen from the protocol by any user because of this vulnerability. A valid cross chain message sent to one chain which mints or unlocks tokens can be replayed on any other EVM chain with the same handler contract addresses, thus allowing an attacker to potentially extract multiple copies of assets.

Other handlers that receive cross chain messages from `ChakraSettlement` and have the same contract addresses across multiple networks would also be exploitable.

Also, as the events of `receive_cross_chain_msg()` would be emitted on each chain, it is possible that off chain systems and bridges that monitor this event could also be exploited.

## Proof of Concept
The function `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_msg()` does not receive the destination chain in its parameters and is therefore unable to check that it is not receiving a replayed message from another chain.

The functions verify signatures, and check the transaction has not been seen before, but then go on to call handlers and emit the event and return `true`. It would therefore be possible for any address to resubmit a valid received cross chain message from another chain. 

However, this would require certain conditions:
1) The validators that have signed the message would need to be valid on both chains.
2) The handler on both receiving chains would need to have the same contract address. However, this is quite possible if they have the same code and were deployed in the same manner.

Within `ChakraSettlementHandler`, its function `receive_cross_chain_msg` would be called by the `ChakraSettlement` contract on this line:
```
bool result = ISettlementHandler(to_handler).receive_cross_chain_msg(
    txid,
    from_chain,
    from_address,
    from_handler,
    payload_type,
    payload,
    sign_type,
    signatures
);
```
The code of `ChakraSettlementHandler.receive_cross_chain_msg()` also has no way to check the chain ID of the received message as the settlement contract does not have this information to pass on.

## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The protocol should include the `to_chainid` in its calls to `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_msg()`.

In `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_msg()` perform a check on the `to_chain` against `block.chainid`.

It is also recommended to pass the `to_chain` to handlers so that they can also potentially check it, although this is an additional layer of security and should not be necessary if `ChakraSettlement` is already checking the destination chain id.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L391-L393
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L328-L330
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L303-L331
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L138-L165


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If the cross chain callback fails for a token transfer, then the sending user's tokens will remain locked in the handler contract on the source chain or, in the case of `BurnUnlock` mode, the user's tokens would remain burned.

If sending from an EVM chain, the callback could register as having failed and `create_cross_txs[txid].status` would be updated, but this does not give the user any way to retrieve their tokens.

Additionally, users may be unwilling to trust the protocol with their assets if they are aware that there is no rescue procedure. So this issue can harm the protocol regardless of how confident the protocol may be in the reliability of the cross chain relaying system.

## Proof of Concept
When initiating a cross chain movement of tokens from either an EVM chain or Starknet, the settlement contract sends a cross chain message and expects a callback confirming the successful receipt of the original message. We will consider two scenarios.

First scenario: no callback message is ever received because the original outgoing message failed.

In this case, for both EVM and Starknet, the tokens would be lost in the initial call to `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`. They would be either locked or burned, depending on the mode. These handler contracts do not provide a mechanism for rescuing these tokens. No tokens would be minted or unlocked on the destination chain, as the message was never received.

It might be submitted that the cross chain message should not simply fail. However, it is quite possible that a network or hardware failure or a misconfiguration of validators on the receiving chain might cause this to happen and some messages might fail to be sent.

Second scenario: the callback message is received, but with a failure status.

In this case, the EVM chains would update `create_cross_txs[txid].status` to `CrossChainTxStatus.Failed` within the function [`receive_cross_chain_callback` (link)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L391-L393). However, this does not give the user any way to retrieve their tokens.

On Starknet, the cairo code processes the callback regardless. This is discussed in another submission.

## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
If a callback is not received after a certain period of time, allow a user to retrieve their tokens from the handler contract.

If a callback is received and it has a failure status for a pending status transaction, allow a user to retrieve their tokens from the handler contract after a cooldown period.



## Assessed type

Error

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L395-L417
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L393-L415
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L138-L165


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
For a handler operating in mode `MintBurn`, a cross chain message for a failed callback will still burn the user's tokens from the handler contract. This means that a user has transferred their tokens to the handler contract as part of a call to `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` in expectation of tokens being minted by the Chakra handler on the destination chain. However, the failed callback status is a good indication that the minting has not happened. In this case, the user's tokens are burnt when they should be returned to them.

## Proof of Concept
The functions `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_msg()` receive the parameter `cross_chain_msg_status` but do not perform any check on the value of this parameter. It is used to calculate `message_hash_final` which is used to check signatures, but this is not dependant on the status being of a successful message transmission.

Instead, the handler is called on this line:
```
let success = handler.receive_cross_chain_callback(cross_chain_msg_id, from_chain, to_chain, from_handler, to_handler , cross_chain_msg_status);
```
As can be seen, the handler does receive the message status, but in `ERC20Handler.receive_cross_chain_callback()`, there is no check on the value of `cross_chain_msg_status` and tokens are burned:
```
if self.mode.read() == SettlementMode::MintBurn{
erc20.burn_from(get_contract_address(), self.created_tx.read(cross_chain_msg_id).amount);
}
```

## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The protocol team must determine as a design decision whether they want this check to be processed in handlers or the settlement contract.

The handler seems like the more appropriate location, as this allows the release of locked assets. In this case, it is vital that any handler checks the value of `cross_chain_msg_status` and reacts accordingly.

In the specific case of a failed status in the handler `ERC20Handler`, the contract needs to release locked tokens or mint any tokens that have already been burned. It also needs to dynamically update the status it writes on [line 161](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L161) to a failed status where appropriate.

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/BaseSettlement.sol#L121-L127


# Vulnerability details


## Impact
The `set_required_validators_num` function allows any address with the `MANAGER_ROLE` to set the `required_validators` to an invalid value. Since the `MANAGER_ROLE` is not a trusted role, this could lead to two critical issues:
1. Setting `required_validators` to zero, which would disable the validation mechanism entirely.
2. Setting `required_validators` to a value greater than the current number of validators (`validator_count`), making it impossible to reach consensus and halting the contract's operations.

This could result in a denial of service (DoS) or a complete breakdown of the validation system, as the contract would be unable to function correctly without a valid number of validators.

## Proof of Concept
 `set_required_validators_num` function does not include any checks to ensure that the new value for `required_validators` is valid:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/BaseSettlement.sol#L121-L127

```solidity
function set_required_validators_num(
    uint256 _required_validators
) external onlyRole(MANAGER_ROLE) {
    uint256 old = required_validators;
    required_validators = _required_validators;
    emit RequiredValidatorsChanged(msg.sender, old, required_validators);
}
```

### Issue 1: Setting `required_validators` to zero
A manager could call the function with `_required_validators = 0`, effectively disabling the validation mechanism, as no validators would be required to approve transactions.

### Issue 2: Setting `required_validators` higher than `validator_count`
A manager could set `_required_validators` to a value greater than the current number of validators (`validator_count`). This would make it impossible to reach the required number of validator approvals, potentially halting the contract's operations.


## Tools used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
implement strict checks within the `set_required_validators_num` function. Ensure that the new value is greater than zero and does not exceed the current total validator count. Alternatively, consider implementing a multi-signature or time-lock mechanism for changing critical parameters like `required_validators`, especially given that managers are not trusted roles.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`message_hash` is incorrectly computed, which will not allow signature verification.

## Proof of Concept

The `message_hash` that validators will sign to execute `receive_cross_chain_msg()` contains 2 fields (`payload` and `from_chain`) that are dynamic types (`bytes` and `string`).

```solidity
function receive_cross_chain_msg(
    uint256 txid,
    string memory from_chain,
    uint256 from_address,
    uint256 from_handler,
    address to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type,
    bytes calldata payload,
    uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
    bytes calldata signatures // signature array
) external {
    {
        // verify signature
        bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(
                txid,
                from_chain, // AUDIT - missing keccak256
                from_address,
                from_handler,
                to_handler,
                keccak256(payload)
            )
        );
```

When a parameter of either of these two types is used in `message_hash`, its `keccak256` result must be used, since the value of these types is `dynamic`.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

```diff
function receive_cross_chain_msg(
    uint256 txid,
    string memory from_chain,
    uint256 from_address,
    uint256 from_handler,
    address to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type,
    bytes calldata payload,
    uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
    bytes calldata signatures // signature array
) external {
    {
        // verify signature
        bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(
                txid,
-               from_chain,
+               keccak256(from_chain),
                from_address,
                from_handler,
                to_handler,
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111-L223


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Cross-chain tx do not enforce order (`nonce`), making them vulnerable to block reorgs.

## Proof of Concept

Every cross-chain tx starts via `Handler.cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` and the `CrossChainMsg` event emitted by `Settlement.send_cross_chain_msg()` is what validators will watch for to continue the flow on the destination chain.

```solidity
function send_cross_chain_msg(
    string memory to_chain,
    address from_address,
    uint256 to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type,
    bytes calldata payload
) external {
    require(msg.sender == handler, "Not Handler");

    nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;

    address from_handler = msg.sender;

    uint256 txid = uint256(
        keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(
                contract_chain_name, // from chain
                to_chain,
                from_address, // msg.sender address
                from_handler, // settlement handler address
                to_handler,
                nonce_manager[from_address]
            )
        )
    );

    create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
        txid,
        contract_chain_name,
        to_chain,
        from_address,
        from_handler,
        to_handler,
        payload,
        CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending
    );

    emit CrossChainMsg(
        txid,
        from_address,
        contract_chain_name,
        to_chain,
        from_handler,
        to_handler,
        payload_type,
        payload
    );
}
```

But all these cross-chain tx have no enforced parameter like `nonce` to order them, ensuring that the first created will be the first processed.

This will not guarantee that if user A deposits X amount of `USDC` to Polygon, he will be the one to receive it on Optimism if another user also transfers the same shortly after him, but his event is processed first.

Although, if validators execute all transactions in their event broadcast order based on the blockchain explorer, in case of block reorganizations the user tx will be ordered differently than the original one, and since there are no values that provide an order, the first user might not get their funds on the destination chain there aren’t enough, even if they were first.

Since the chains include Polygon, block reorgs problems are possible. Here is a proof:

Polygon: https://polygonscan.com/block/36757444/f?hash=0xf9aefee3ea0e4fc5f67aac48cb6e25912158ce9dca9ec6c99259d937433d6df8 - Dec 2022, this is with 120 blocks depth which means 4 minutes of re-written tx's since the block rate is ~2 seconds

https://protos.com/polygon-hit-by-157-block-reorg-despite-hard-fork-to-reduce-reorgs/ - February 2023, 157 blocks depth.

We can also observe the LayerZero idea for the same type of protocol (cross-chain infrastructure contracts). They always use a `nonce` for all their events to ensure that the logic in the destination chains is in the same sequence as it was initiated in the source chain - https://github.com/LayerZero-Labs/LayerZero/blob/a1fb11a3b9c0ac449291816e71eacede4e36613e/contracts/Endpoint.sol#L94, https://github.com/LayerZero-Labs/LayerZero/blob/a1fb11a3b9c0ac449291816e71eacede4e36613e/contracts/UltraLightNodeV2.sol#L135

> ***NOTE:** Everything described above also applies to the Cairo part and the problem should be fixed there also.*
> 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Include a `nonce` in the events to ensure they are executed in the same way as in the source chain.


## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L183-L192


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

If the `ChakraSettlementHandlers` are all deployed on the same addresses with the `CREATE2` opcode, cross-chain replays will be possible.

## Proof of Concept

In order cross-chain message to arrive at the destination, a set of validators should sign a special `message_hash` that contains all the important params to prevent replaying the tx except one: destination contract’s `contract_chain_name`:

[ChakraSettlement.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170C5-L193C1)

```solidity
function receive_cross_chain_msg(
    uint256 txid,
    string memory from_chain,
    uint256 from_address,
    uint256 from_handler,
    address to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type,
    bytes calldata payload,
    uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
    bytes calldata signatures // signature array
) external {
    {
        // verify signature
        bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(
                txid,
                from_chain,
                from_address,
                from_handler,
                to_handler,
                keccak256(payload)
            )
        );
```

As we can see, nowhere destination chain is passed to the hash and once signed by the validators, it can be used by malicious users to be replayed across all the `to_handlers`.

Another pre-condition that is needed is for the `to_handler` to have the same address on the other chain as well, which will be most likely the case because contracts are identical and can be deployed like that.

When `to_handlers` are the same, replays are possible because currently, all the params of the hash are destination chain agnostic. ChakraSettlement has another replay protection which will be effectively bypassed because on another chain there won’t be a record with that `txid`:

[ChakraSettlement.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L199C13-L202C15)

```solidity
require(
      receive_cross_txs[txid].status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Unknow,
      "Invalid transaction status"
  );

```

The impact of replaying cross-chain transactions will be that the user will be able to mint/unlock the X times the number of tokens that he has locked in the source chain, where X is the number of handlers that have the same address.

Example of an attack:

1. `SettlementMode` is `LockMint`
2. User locks 1e18 tokens in chain A to chain B
3. Transaction is signed by the validators and is executed by trusted parties, the user receives 1e18 tokens on chain B
4. 3 more `ChakraSettlementHandler` contracts have the same address as the handler on chain B
5. The user manually replays the transaction across these 3 handlers, receiving 4e18 tokens in total.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Include the `contract_chain_name` or `chain_id` in the `message_hash`:

```diff
bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
    abi.encodePacked(
        txid,
        from_chain,
        from_address,
        from_handler,
        to_handler,
+       contract_chain_name,
+       chain_id,
        keccak256(payload)
    )
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/ckr_btc.cairo#L199-L206


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When the new balance is not equal to the old balance plus the amount, the function will return false without reverting.

## Proof of Concept

The mint_to function is designed to mint new tokens to a specified address. However, its implementation allows for a scenario where tokens are minted successfully, but the function returns false, indicating a failure withoug reverting. 

```
      fn mint_to(ref self: ContractState, to: ContractAddress, amount: u256) -> bool {
            let caller = get_caller_address();
            assert(self.chakra_operators.read(caller) == 1, Errors::NOT_OPERATOR);
            let old_balance = self.erc20.balance_of(to);
            self.erc20.mint(to, amount);
            let new_balance = self.erc20.balance_of(to);
            return new_balance == old_balance + amount;
        }
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/ckr_btc.cairo#L199-L206

- The function checks if the caller is an authorized operator.
- It records the old balance of the recipient.
- It calls the mint function to create new tokens.
- It checks the new balance of the recipient.
- It returns a boolean value based on whether the new balance equals the old balance plus the minted amount.

However, when the function returns "false", it doesn't revert.

Consider the following sequence of events:

* Alice's balance: 5,000 tokens
* Call mint_to(alice_address, 1000)
* Internal minting operation succeeds
* Due to some reasons, Alice's balance is not updated
* Function execution:
```
let old_balance = self.erc20.balance_of(alice_address);  // Returns 5,000
self.erc20.mint(alice_address, 1000);  // Succeeds, actual total supply is now 1,001,000
let new_balance = self.erc20.balance_of(alice_address);  // Returns 5,000 due to delayed update
return new_balance == old_balance + amount;  // Returns false (5,000 != 5,000 + 1,000)
```

* Function returns false and doesn't revert

Similar issue is in burn_from function:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/ckr_btc.cairo#L216

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Revert on Failure:

```
fn mint_to(ref self: ContractState, to: ContractAddress, amount: u256) {
    // ... existing code ...
    assert(new_balance == old_balance + amount, Errors::MINT_FAILED);
}
```





## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L174


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Complete DoS in `setttlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()` and `settlement::receive_cross_chain_callback()` when validator/proposer calls these function as the signature componet `r` and `s` would not fit in `felt252`.
This is a critical issue as it will completely disrupts the protocol on starknet side.

## Proof of Concept
The `settlement::check_chakra_signatures()` implements a signature verification logic using starknet corelib `ecdsa.cairo`.
The implementation recovers the public key of validator using the message_hash and the signature component v, r, s then it compares it to the saved public key of the validator, if matched the pass_count is incremented and if required number of pass_count is reached then the verification is successfull.

The `settlement::check_chakra_signatures()` takes signatures as array of : `Array<(felt252, felt252, bool)`. The settlement contract also stores the validator public key as type felt252 `chakra_validators_pubkey: LegacyMap<felt252, u8>`

However this implementation for verifying signature is incorrect and will lead to revert of transaction when validator/proposer calls `setttlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()` or `settlement::receive_cross_chain_callback()` because of the working of `ecdsa.cairo` ( the corelib used by `settlement.cairo` contract) which slightly deviates from the standard ecdsa.
Reference : https://github.com/starkware-libs/cairo/blob/main/corelib/src/ecdsa.cairo#L13

The Chakra Validator network uses ecdsa `Seck256k1` algorithm to sign the message on offchain then sumbit it onchain for all the blockchain networks including Starkent. However due to differences in how starknet corelib `ecdsa.cairo` implements ecdsa, the curve used by this library is `STRAK_CURVE` and its order is `STARK_ORDER` which is different and smaller then order used for `Secp256k1` .
- `STARK_ORDER` ( `p` ) = `3618502788666131213697322783095070105623107215331596699973092056135872020481` [ 252 bits ]
- `Secp256k1_ORDER` ( `n` )= `115792089237316195423570985008687907852837564279074904382605163141518161494337` [ 256 bits ]
- and `STARK_ORDER` < `Secp256k1_ORDER`

Since the Chakra Validator network uses ecdsa `Seck256k1` the range for `r` and `s` of signature is `[ 1, n - 1 ]` . Because of this the values of `r` and `s` can be greater than `p` which will not fit in `felt252` which is expected in `settlement::check_chakra_signatures()`. This will cause revert of the transaction.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Fixing this issue require changes in the design of signature verification in `settlement::check_chakra_signatures()`. It needs to implement a signature verification logic which uses ecdsa `Secp256k1_ORDER`.
For this protocol can consider using the starknet corelib `eth_signature.cairo` library which uses the `secp256k1` curve.
Reference to library : https://github.com/starkware-libs/cairo/blob/main/corelib/src/starknet/eth_signature.cairo
Also in `settlement.cairo` the storage mapping  `chakra_validators_pubkey: LegacyMap<felt252, u8>,` needs to be changed to `chakra_validators_pubkey: LegacyMap<u256, u8>,` as public key in `secp256k1` curve is of 256 bits.





## Assessed type

DoS
