# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L193


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A malicious/attacker validator can steal token from pool or can cause other distruption in the protcol normal working flow as the malicious/attacker validator have full control to craft any malicious message and use it over ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback() or ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()

## Proof of Concept

The SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol implements internal function verifyECDSA() which is invoked/used two times during ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg() and ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback().
However function verifyECDSA() doesn't check for uniqueness in signatures array which makes it vulnerable to signature replay attack.

The system design for Chakra protocol is that between two chains chakra validator network is involved which listen for onchain messaing event, interecpts it and signs it then calls the receive_cross_chain_callback() or receive_cross_chain_msg() as per the nature of message.
These are the workings/propertise of chakra validator network as mentioned by their developer/docs.

- Anyone can permissionlessly become validator in chakra network by staking enough tokens.
- Validator network listen for ChakraSettlement::CrossChainMsg event then calls the respective receive_cross_chain_msg() of the destination chain.
- Validator network also listen for ChakraSettlement::CrossChainHandleResult event then calls the respective receive_cross_chain_callback() of the source chain.
- Validators are consensused, each validator performs the same operation and maintains the same state. Each round will select a proposer, and the proposer will call receive_cross_chain_msg() or receive_cross_chain_callback() depending on nature of message with message hash and signatures of all the other validator.
- Proposer is choosen from the set of validators using DPoS.
- If required number of validator is acheived onchain, the transaction is accpeted by the contract.
A malicious/attacker validator will wait for its turn to be chosen proposer to call the receive_cross_chain_msg(). The malicious/attacker validator will crafts its own custom malicious message signs it, use the same signature for the signatrues calldata while calling receive_cross_chain_msg().

As malicious/attacker validator will be registered onchain, so ```validators[msgHash.recover(sig)] && ++m >= required_validators``` will hold true. And due to lack of uniqueness check in signatures array, the attacker can inflate the `m` count and evetually satisfy the condition
```
if (
       validators[msgHash.recover(sig)] && ++m >= required_validators
   ) 
```
[https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L193](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L193)

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The internal function SettlementSignatureVerifier::check_chakra_signatures() should implement and efficient logic to ensure only unique signatures are used.





## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to maintain a mapping of Chain to tokenId for source and destination chains. The mapping is managed by either the owner or through governance.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L193


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Reusing a valid signature may result in funds being diverted

SettlementSignatureVerifier contract.In the verifyECDSA method, the signature verification process does not check for the uniqueness of each signature. Since validators[msgHash.recover(sig)] only checks whether the recovered signer is a validator, an attacker could reuse the same signature multiple times to meet the required required_validators threshold. This could allow an attacker to pass the multi-signature verification with fewer distinct validators than required, potentially leading to the unauthorized transfer of all funds in the contract or misuse of contract functionality.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L193

In the following code:

```

for (uint256 i = 0; i < len; i += 65) {
    bytes memory sig = signatures[i:i + 65];
    if (validators[msgHash.recover(sig)] && ++m >= required_validators) {
        return true;
    }
}
```

The code loops through signatures and uses `msgHash.recover(sig)` to extract the signer. It checks if the recovered signer is a validator, but does not ensure that each signature comes from a different validator. This allows an attacker to reuse a single validator's signature multiple times to satisfy the verification requirements.

## Tools Used

VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a uniqueness check for signatures in the `verifyECDSA` method. This can be done by tracking validated signers to ensure each signature comes from a distinct validator.

Use a `mapping` or array to store the signers already verified in the current verification process to prevent signature reuse.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L125


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The remove_validator method allows the status of all validators to be set to false, which will cause the contract to fail to pass the signature verification logic and the system will no longer be able to operate normally.

SettlementSignatureVerifier contract.  The `remove_validator` method allows setting all validators to `false`, which could cause `validators[msgHash.recover(sig)]` to fail. This means that even if a signature is valid, the contract will be unable to verify it because there would be no validators available. This could lead to a complete failure of the contract's multi-signature functionalities, making it impossible to execute crucial actions such as transferring assets or performing critical operations.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L125

In the `remove_validator` method:

```

function remove_validator(
    address validator
) external onlyRole(MANAGER_ROLE) {
    require(validators[validator] == true, "Validator does not exists");
    validators[validator] = false;
    validator_count -= 1;
    emit ValidatorRemoved(msg.sender, validator);
}
```

This code allows the removal of all validators. If all validators are removed, the `validators` mapping will have no valid entries, and even correct signatures will fail to match any validators, breaking the `verifyECDSA` function's logic.

## Tools Used

VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1. Introduce a restriction that ensures at least one validator is always present in the system when removing validators, preventing the system from losing its validation capability.
2. Check the `validator_count` variable before removal to ensure the number of remaining validators is above a minimum safe threshold.


## Assessed type

DoS

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L83


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The remove_validator method allows the status of all validators to be set to false, which will cause the contract to fail to pass the signature verification logic and the system will no longer be able to operate normally.

SettlementSignatureVerifier contract.  The `remove_validator` method allows setting all validators to `false`, which could cause `validators[msgHash.recover(sig)]` to fail. This means that even if a signature is valid, the contract will be unable to verify it because there would be no validators available. This could lead to a complete failure of the contract's multi-signature functionalities, making it impossible to execute crucial actions such as transferring assets or performing critical operations.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/SettlementSignatureVerifier.sol#L83

In the `remove_validator` method:

```

function remove_validator(
    address validator
) external onlyRole(MANAGER_ROLE) {
    require(validators[validator] == true, "Validator does not exists");
    validators[validator] = false;
    validator_count -= 1;
    emit ValidatorRemoved(msg.sender, validator);
}
```

This code allows the removal of all validators. If all validators are removed, the `validators` mapping will have no valid entries, and even correct signatures will fail to match any validators, breaking the `verifyECDSA` function's logic.

## Tools Used

VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1. Introduce a restriction that ensures at least one validator is always present in the system when removing validators, preventing the system from losing its validation capability.
2. Check the `validator_count` variable before removal to ensure the number of remaining validators is above a minimum safe threshold.





## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L405


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The bug will cause the cross-chain callback to fail when the `chain_name` is changed at source after a cross-chain tx has been sent.

## Proof of Concept
When initiating a cross chain ERC20 settlement, the  [`from_chain` is given as follows](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L170):
```solidity
    let from_chain = settlement.chain_name();
```
This is then [saved for the transaction](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L186) as follows:
```solidity
            let tx: CreatedCrossChainTx = CreatedCrossChainTx{
                    tx_id: tx_id,
>>                  from_chain: from_chain,
                    ---SNIP---
                };
>>          self.created_tx.write(tx_id, tx);
```

Also, the protocol has [`set_chain_name()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L472-L475) function used to change this `chain_name`:
```solidity
        fn set_chain_name(ref self: ContractState, chain_name: felt252){
            self.ownable.assert_only_owner();
            self.chain_name.write(chain_name);
        }
```

The issue then arises during cross chain callback:

- `receive_cross_chain_callback()`:
This function handles callbacks for cross-chain transactions that were initiated from this contract and are now responding back after processing on another chain.

It performs the following [check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L405):
```solidity
    assert(self.created_tx.read(cross_chain_msg_id).from_chain == to_chain, 'from_chain error');
```
From this, the function will revert:

**Scenario**:
1. When initiating a cross-chain `tx1` the following parameters are used:
- `from_chain`: `chainA`
- `to_chain`: `chainD`
2. After this tx is sent, the owner calls `set_chain_name()` at source and changes the `chain_name` from  `chainA` to  `chainB`.
3. After processing `tx1` on `chainD` a callback is to be received at source chain (`chainB`), previously `chainA`.
4. Due to the checks above, `to_chain`(`chainB`) is supposed to be the same as `from_chain` that was saved for `tx1` during initialization (`chainA`) but this is not the case.
5. The `chain_name` has changed and as such, the callback will fail with `'from_chain error'`.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
This is tough one.
1. Delete the `set_chain_name()` entirely and only rely on its [initialization in the `constructor()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L165)
2. Impelement another way to validate authenticity of these callback messages






## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/TokenRoles.sol#L10
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/TokenRoles.sol#L19-L23


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The lack of proper `upgradeability` setup introduces operational risks, as the contract may not behave as expected during upgrade attempts, leading to potential downtime or service disruptions.

## Proof of Concept
The `TokenRoles` contract [inherits from `UUPSUpgradeable`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/TokenRoles.sol#L10), a contract from `OpenZeppelin` that provides `upgradeability` features.
```solidity
    abstract contract TokenRoles is
        OwnableUpgradeable,
>>      UUPSUpgradeable,
        AccessControlUpgradeable
    {
```
This standard requires certain initialization steps to be performed to ensure the contract is properly set up for upgrades.

However during initialization, the `__UUPSUpgradeable_init()` function is not called within the [`__TokenRoles_init()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/TokenRoles.sol#L19-L23) function.
```solidity
    function __TokenRoles_init(address _owner, address _operator) public {
        __Ownable_init(_owner);
        _grantRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, _owner);
        _grantRole(OPERATOR_ROLE, _operator);
    }
```
This omission leaves the upgrade mechanism improperly configured.

Since [`ChakraToken` contract inherits from `TokenRoles`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraToken.sol#L14), this contract will not be upgreadable:
---> The `UUPSUpgradeable` contract relies on an internal function [`_authorizeUpgrade()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraToken.sol#L42-L44) in `ChakraToken` contract to control who can upgrade the contract. Without proper initialization, the upgrade authorization mechanism may not function as intended, potentially preventing upgrades.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that the `__UUPSUpgradeable_init()` function is called during initialization
```diff
    function __TokenRoles_init(address _owner, address _operator) public {
        __Ownable_init(_owner);
        _grantRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, _owner);
        _grantRole(OPERATOR_ROLE, _operator);
+       __UUPSUpgradeable_init();
    }
```





## Assessed type

Upgradable

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L216
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L318


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If `to_handler` is not the correct address, the returned boolean could possibly be incorrect. This means that the state update will be incorrect, potentially leading inconsistencies i.e `CrossChainMsgStatus` and `receive_cross_txs[txid].status` could be updated incorrectly.

## Proof of Concept
When receiving cross chain messages, the `to_handler` parameter should point to the receiving contract (`address(this)`).
This is validated in [`handler_erc20::receive_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L110) and [`handler_erc20::receive_cross_chain_callback()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L140) as follows:
```solidity
    assert(to_handler == get_contract_address(),'error to_handler');
```
These functions are called from `settlement` contract  and therefore has to validate that indeed the `to_handler` is the receiving address.
[`settlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L354-L356)
```solidity
            
>>   let handler = IHandlerDispatcher{contract_address: to_handler};
>>   let success = handler.receive_cross_chain_msg(cross_chain_msg_id, from_chain, to_chain, from_handler, to_handler , payload);

```
[`settlement::receive_cross_chain_callback()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L416-L417)
```solidity
>>    let handler = IHandlerDispatcher{contract_address: to_handler};
>>    let success = handler.receive_cross_chain_callback(cross_chain_msg_id, from_chain, to_chain, from_handler, to_handler ,  cross_chain_msg_status);
```

However, in [`ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L216) and [`ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L318), the `to_handler`  passed to the call but is never validated as the handler functions ([`ChackraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_msg()`]() & [`ChackraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_callback()`]()) do not perform this validation.

Notice that when [saving received cross chain transaction](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L211), `ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()` uses `address(this)` as the `to_handler` without really verifying that it points to it.
```solidity
        receive_cross_txs[txid] = ReceivedCrossChainTx(
            txid,
            from_chain,
            contract_chain_name,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
>>          address(this),
            payload,
            CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending
        );
```

Note that the  boolean returned from the calls determines the  state update in `ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()` and `ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback()`.

---> If `to_handler` is not the correct address, the returned boolean could possibly be incorrect. This means that the state update will be incorrect, potentially leading inconsistencies i.e `CrossChainMsgStatus` and `receive_cross_txs[txid].status` could be updated incorrectly as shown below:
- [`ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L216-L233)
```solidity
>>      bool result = ISettlementHandler(to_handler).receive_cross_chain_msg( //@audit-info Boolean returned
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            payload_type,
            payload,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );

        //@audit-info State updates depend on it
        CrossChainMsgStatus status = CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed;
        if (result == true) {
            status = CrossChainMsgStatus.Success;
            receive_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainMsgStatus.Success;
        } else {
            receive_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed;
        }
```
- [`ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L317-L330)
```solidity
>>      if ( //@audit-info Boolean returned
            ISettlementHandler(to_handler).receive_cross_chain_callback(
                txid,
                from_chain,
                from_handler,
                status,
                sign_type,
                signatures
            )
        ) {
>>          create_cross_txs[txid].status = status; //@audit-info State updates depend on it
        } else {
>>          create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed; //@audit-info State updates depend on it
        }
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To fix this bug, we should validate the `to_handler` address before the call in `ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()` and `ChackraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_msg()`.
```diff
+   require(to_handler == address(this),'error to_handler');
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-L192
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlementUpgradeTest.sol#L136-L158


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Non-compliance with `EIP712` can cause problems with integrators and potentially lead to denial of service.

## Proof of Concept
According to [EIP712 Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712#definition-of-typed-structured-data-%F0%9D%95%8A):
> The dynamic values `bytes` and `string` are encoded as a `keccak256` hash of their contents.

However, in [`ChakraSettlement:receive_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-L192), the hashing is done as follows:
```solidity
    function receive_cross_chain_msg(
        uint256 txid,
>>      string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_address,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload,
        uint8 sign_type, // validators signature type /  multisig or bls sr25519
        bytes calldata signatures // signature array
    ) external {
        {
            // verify signature
            bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    txid,
>>                  from_chain, //@audit-info String
                    from_address,
                    from_handler,
                    to_handler,
                    keccak256(payload)
                )
            );
            ---SNIP---
        }
```
As seen, `from_chain` is a `string` value. However, the hashing (`message_hash`) encodes this value directly and not the `keccak256` hash of its content as required by the standard.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct this as follows:
```diff
            // verify signature
            bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    txid,
-                   from_chain,
+                   keccak256(from_chain),
                    from_address,
                    from_handler,
                    to_handler,
                    keccak256(payload)
                )
            );
```








## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The missing validation of the `to_chain` and `to_handler` during cross-chain ERC20 settlement results in eventual transaction failures and also goes against the protocol requirement that these values must be valid for each other.

## Proof of Concept
In the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` function, the `chain` and `handler` are not validated

The function [`is_valid_handler()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L41-L46) checks if a `handler` is valid for a given `chain`:
```solidity
    function is_valid_handler(
        string memory chain_name,
        uint256 handler
    ) public view returns (bool) {
        return handler_whitelist[chain_name][handler];
    }
```
The same goes for [`is_valid_handler()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L234-L236) which is used in [`handle_erc20::cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L168) to validate the  `to_chain` and  `to_handler` provided during initialization of cross-chain ERC20 settlement
```solidity
    assert(self.support_handler.read((to_chain, to_handler)), 'not support handler');
```

However, in [`ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111), this check is not performed:
The function just uses the `to_chain` and  `to_handler` provided as they are without performing any validations.

As such, an invalid `to_handler` for the given `to_chain` may be used which may result in failed transactions.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Validate the `to_chain` and `to_handler` in the `ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`:
```diff
        require(to_handler != 0, "Invalid to handler address");
        require(to_token != 0, "Invalid to token address");
+       require(is_valid_handler(to_chain, to_handler), "Invalid handler");
```





## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L188


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The cross chain tx details saved in `handle_erc20::cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` is incorrect as the function uses the address of the contract as the `from` address instead of the `caller's address`. 
Depending on the use case, if this information is used, it could result in potential issues.

## Proof of Concept
When initiating a cross-chain ERC20 settlement, the `from` address refers to the address of the `caller`.

In [`ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L158), the caller (`msg.sender`) is used as the `from` address when saving the cross chain tx details:
```solidity
            // Save the cross chain tx
            create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
                txid,
                chain,
                to_chain,
>>              msg.sender, //@audit-info Caller address used.
                ---SNIP---
            );
```
[Here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/BaseSettlementHandler.sol#L57) is `CreatedCrossChainTx` signature.

The same value is used when [creating a erc20 transfer payload](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L183) as `from`:
```solidity
            // Create a erc20 transfer payload
            ERC20TransferPayload memory payload = ERC20TransferPayload(
                ERC20Method.Transfer,
>>              AddressCast.to_uint256(msg.sender),
                ---SNIP---
            );
```
The same is used when emitting [`CrossChainLocked`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L214) event again as the `from` address.


However, in [`handle_erc20::cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L188), the function uses the contract address (`get_contract_address()`) as the `from` address when saving the tx details:
```solidity
        let tx: CreatedCrossChainTx = CreatedCrossChainTx{
                    tx_id: tx_id,
                    from_chain: from_chain,
                    to_chain: to_chain,
>>                  from: get_contract_address(), //@audit-info Contract address used (issue)
                    ---SNIP---
                };
```
Yet when [creating a erc20 transfer payload](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L201), caller (`get_caller_address()`) is used as `from`:
```solidity
        let transfer = ERC20Transfer{
                method_id: 1,
>>              from: contract_address_to_u256(get_caller_address()),
                ---SNIP---
            };
```
And when emitting the [`CrossChainLocked`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L222) event, the caller address is still used as `from`.

As seen above, incorrect information (from address) is saved for the tx.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct this as follows:
```diff
        let tx: CreatedCrossChainTx = CreatedCrossChainTx{
                    tx_id: tx_id,
                    from_chain: from_chain,
                    to_chain: to_chain,
-                   from: get_contract_address(),
+                   from: get_caller_address(), //@audit Use the caller address used.
                    ---SNIP---
                };
```


























## Assessed type

Error

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L186
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L321-L331


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the context of cross-chain transactions, it is crucial to ensure that the `token` received on the destination chain is indeed the one intended by the sender from the source chain. Without this validation at destination:
1. Recipients end up with the wrong token.
2. Chances are that the recipients will therefore have to perform `swaps` to obtain the `intended tokens` which will incur them `fees`. Therefore, the `net value` received will be lower given the fee deductions.

## Proof of Concept
One of the `Main invariants` in `Settlement Handler Contract` is this:
> Only the specified token contract (set during initialization) can be used for transfers, mints, and burns within this handler.

As such, when users lock/burn tokens at the source, only specified token at the destination will be minted/unlocked for the recipient.

During initiatiation of a cross-chain ERC20 settlement in `ChackraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement()`, the user who wishes to lock/burn their tokens specifies the [`to_token`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L114) which they want to be unlocked/minted at the `destination` for the recipient.
This `to_token` is then included in the [`ERC20TransferPayload`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L186):
```solidity
            // Create a erc20 transfer payload
            ERC20TransferPayload memory payload = ERC20TransferPayload(
                ERC20Method.Transfer,
                AddressCast.to_uint256(msg.sender),
                to,
                AddressCast.to_uint256(token),
>>              to_token,
                amount
            );
```

However, in the `receive_cross_chain_msg()` function, the `to_token` is not checked to be the configured token at destination. The [`ChackraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L321-L331) decodes the transfer payload then simply proceeds to mint/unlock `transfer_payload.amount` of the `token` configured at destination to the recipient (`transfer_payload.to`).
```solidity
                // Decode transfer payload
                ERC20TransferPayload memory transfer_payload = codec
                    .deocde_transfer(msg_payload);

                if (mode == SettlementMode.MintBurn) {
                    _erc20_mint(
>>                      AddressCast.to_address(transfer_payload.to),
>>                      transfer_payload.amount
                    );
                    return true;
                }
                ---SNIP---
                function _erc20_mint(address account, uint256 amount) internal {
>>                  IERC20Mint(token).mint_to(account, amount); //@audit-info `token` configured at destination
                }
```
The issue arises when the recipient expects `tokenA` but gets minted/unlocked `tokenB`

## Scenario
- `Bob` locks `USDC` at source
- He specifies `to_token` as `USDT`
- At destination, the configured token is `WETH`
- `Alice` (recipient) expects to be minted `USDT` but winds up with `WETH`

**Other instances**:
- [`handler_erc20::receive_cross_chain_msg()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L120-L133)

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Validate the `to_token` at destination to ensure it matches the `token` configured at destination.
Revert if these tokens do not match.
- `ChackraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_msg()`
```diff
        // Decode transfer payload
        ERC20TransferPayload memory transfer_payload = codec
            .deocde_transfer(msg_payload);

+       require(transfer_payload.to_token == token, "Invalid destination token");

        // @audit Proceed with minting/unlocking
        ---SNIP--
```

- `handler_erc20::receive_cross_chain_msg()`
```diff
    let payload_transfer = message.payload;
    let transfer = decode_transfer(payload_transfer);
    ---SNIP---
    let token = IERC20Dispatcher{contract_address: self.token_address.read()};
+   assert(token == transfer.to_token, 'Invalid destination token');   
```














## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/BaseSettlementHandler.sol#L113


# Vulnerability details

## Description: 
In `BaseSettlementHandler.sol` and `BaseSettlement.sol`, the `_Settlement_handler_init` function and `_Settlement_init` function don't have any initializer modifier or any access control respectively and these are public functions, because of this anyone can call these function and manipulate state of the contract. These functions are responsible for initializing critical state variables of the protocol like Owner, settlement, verifier, mode, token, chain, managers, chain name, chained, and other important variables.

An Attacker can call the `_Settlement_handler_init` function and can manipulate the `mode` state variable and then the attacker can send a transaction from `ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement` with any amount and if the `mode` variable is not intended according to function Then the transaction will become successful and Attacker can take that amount of funds from another chain.

## Impact: 
Potential for unauthorized parties to control the contract completely. State Manipulation, Business Logic Disruption, Loss of Funds, Incorrect Cross-Chain Transactions, Ownership Takeover, Reinitialization Attack, Upgradeability Exploit

## Scenario Breakdown:

- During Initialization :

  - The `initialize` function is called with proper arguments, and it internally calls `_Settlement_handler_init` to set key state variables (such as owner, token, settlement, etc.).

  - The `initializer` modifier ensures that this initialization logic is executed only once.

- After Initialization :

  - The `initialize` function cannot be called again.

  - However, since `_Settlement_handler_init` is a public function, it remains exposed. Anyone can call `_Settlement_handler_init` directly and reinitialize critical state variables like owner, token, settlement, etc.

  - This leads to a vulnerability where an attacker can call `_Settlement_handler_init` and reinitialize the contract, taking control of the contract and manipulating important functionality.

## Proof of Concept:
For State Manipulation, Ownership Takeover, Reinitialization Attack, Upgradeability Exploit :

- An attacker can call the `BaseSettlementHandler::_Settlement_handler_init` and `BaseSettlement::_Settlement_init` functions to manipulate the state and reinitialize the contracts because these functions don't have any access control and it is public.

For Loss of Funds, Incorrect Cross-chain Transactions :

1. An attacker reinitializes the `BaseSettlementHandler::_Settlement_handler_init` function.
2. Attacker changes `mode` to anything like 4 and enums in Solidity are treated as their underlying integer representation, and Solidity doesn't perform automatic bounds checking when assigning values to enums.
3. Now the attacker calls `ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement` this function with unexpected `mode` and any amount they need on another chain. Also, this function is not payable.
4. According to the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement` function, funds are only deposited into this contract when `mode` is MintBurn, LockUnlock, LockMint, BurnUnlock.
5. In this case, an attacker can claim any amount of money on another chain
   See [cross_chain_erc20_settlement](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111).

## Recommended Mitigation:

1. Add the `initializer` Modifier to `_Settlement_handler_init` and `_Settlement_init` to ensure it can only be called once.
2. Add Access Control (e.g., onlyOwner) to restrict who can call `_Settlement_handler_init directly`.
3. Make `_Settlement_handler_init` Internal to prevent external calls.





## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L391


# Vulnerability details

## Description: 
 When a cross-chain transaction fails on the destination chain, the source chain should refund the user's amount. However, in the given implementation, the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function in `ChakraSettlementHandler` does not include any logic for refunds when the transaction status is Failed. Consequently, the source chain's `receive_cross_chain_callback` does not trigger any refund mechanism upon receiving a failed status.


## Impact: 
Loss of funds for user and locking of funds in protocol. There is no way to take this money out. The failure to refund user funds can lead to financial losses for users, which could undermine trust in the system. If users are not refunded in the event of a failure, it directly affects their assets and could lead to significant financial implications.

## Proof of Concept:
1. Scenario Setup:

    - A user initiates a cross-chain transaction from the source chain to the destination chain.
    - The handler on the destination chain is not whitelisted on the source chain, leading to a failed status for the transaction.
  
2. Observation:

    - On the destination chain, the transaction status is set to Failed, but there is no refund mechanism in place.
    - The `receive_cross_chain_callback` function on the source chain does not refund the user's amount even though the status is    Failed.
  
3. Expected Behavior:

    - If the transaction fails, the source chain should process a refund to the user.
  
4. Demonstration:

    - A transaction is initiated with an amount (e.g., 100 tokens).
    - The transaction fails on the destination chain.
    - The user's 100 tokens are not refunded to their account on the source chain.

## Recommended Mitigation:
Implement Refund Logic: Modify the `ChakraSettlementHandler` contract to include a refund mechanism in the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function when a Failed status is encountered.








## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374


# Vulnerability details

## Description: 
When a cross-chain transaction successful on the destination chain. However, in the given implementation, the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function in `ChakraSettlementHandler` does not include any logic for withdraw money which is not going to burn because when the `from_handler` from destination chain is not whitelisted on source chain. Consequently, the source chain's `receive_cross_chain_callback` does not trigger any withdraw mechanism upon receiving a not whitelisted handler from destination chain.

In other words, the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function in `ChakraSettlementHandler` checks if the `from_handler` is whitelisted using the `is_valid_handler` function. If the `from_handler` is not whitelisted, the function returns false without further processing. This can cause funds to be locked on the source chain without any withdraw or resolution for the user.

## Impact: 
If a `from_handler` is not whitelisted on the destination chain but the transaction was successful on the source chain, the user’s funds never burned on the source chain and never withdrawed from the source chain. This results in permanent loss of funds or locking of assets. Then this `create_cross_txs[txid].amount` variable always have amounts which aren't able to withdraw. 

## Proof of Concept:
1. Scenario Setup:

    - A user initiates a cross-chain transaction from the source chain to the destination chain.
    - The transaction is marked as successful on the source chain (funds are burned).
    - On the source chain, the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function detects that the `from_handler` is not whitelisted.
    - Locking of protocol funds because not burned in callback functionality even when amount minted to user on destination chain.
  
2. Steps : 
    - A user deposits an amount (e.g., 100 tokens) on the source chain and initiates a cross-chain transaction.
    - The source chain successfully processes the transaction, and the user’s funds are burned.
    - The destination chain recieve and sent acknowledge to source chain that transaction went successful.
    - When the source chain attempts to process the callback, it returns false because the `from_handler` is not whitelisted.
    - No burned is triggered, and the funds remain locked, with no resolution for the protocol and user to withdraw funds anyway.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374


# Vulnerability details

## Description:
In `ChakraSettlementHandler::receive_cross_chain_callback` function, if transaction went successful on source chain and destination chain and when callback functionality hits then even if a `from_handler` from `from_chain` is not whitelisted on source chain. The funds minted to `to` address on destination chain and not burned from source chain.

The vulnerability lies in the `receive_cross_chain_callback` function of `ChakraSettlementHandler`. The issue occurs when a cross-chain transaction is successful on both the source and destination chains, but the callback logic checks whether the `from_handler` from the `from_chain` is whitelisted. If the `from_handler` is not whitelisted, the protocol allows funds to be minted on the destination chain without burning the corresponding amount from the source chain. This breaks a key invariant of the protocol, which expects the funds on the source chain to be burned when they are minted on the destination chain, and leads to locking of funds on the source chain.

## Impact: 
Amount of funds minted successfuly on destination chain even if `from_handler` detected not whitelisted on source chain callback functionality, breaks Main invariant of protocol and locking of funds as funds on source chain not burned.

## Proof of Concept:
1. User initiates a cross-chain transfer of 100 tokens from SourceChain to DestinationChain. Both the source chain and destination chain contracts are configured, but the `from_handler` on SourceChain callback functionality is not whitelisted.
2. The transaction is marked as Success on the source chain. The source chain processes the transaction. The destination chain is already minted the corresponding amount for the user.
3. The callback is triggered on the source chain (`receive_cross_chain_callback`). The callback logic detects that the `from_handler` from destination chain is not whitelisted. However, the code does not revert or prevent the minting of tokens on the destination chain.
4. Despite the `from_handler` not being whitelisted, the destination chain successfully mints 100 tokens to the user’s address on DestinationChain.
5. On the source chain, the funds are not burned because the callback function detects that the `from_handler` is not whitelisted. The transaction is left in an inconsistent state, where the user’s funds are locked on the source chain, but they also have successfully minted tokens on the destination chain.
6. The user now has 100 tokens on the destination chain (minted), while the same amount is still locked on the source chain, breaking the protocol's invariant of burning tokens on the source chain when they are minted on the destination chain.

## Tool Used:
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation: If the `from_handler` is not whitelisted, the transaction should revert on both chains or initiate a refund.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L127-L128


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Unauthorized Caller would Send Cross Chain Messages due to absence of msg.sender validation as against Protocol expectation
## Proof of Concept
```solidity
function send_cross_chain_msg(
        string memory to_chain,
        address from_address,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload
    ) external {
        nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;

        address from_handler = msg.sender;

        uint256 txid = uint256(
            keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    contract_chain_name, // from chain
                    to_chain,
>>>                    from_address, // msg.sender address
>>>                    from_handler, // settlement handler address
                    to_handler,
                    nonce_manager[from_address]
                )
            )
        );

        create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
            txid,
            contract_chain_name,
            to_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            payload,
            CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending
        );

        emit CrossChainMsg(
            ...
        );
    }
```
The code above shows how send_cross_chain_msg is implemented in the ChakraSettlement contract, it can be noted from the pointer in the code above that "from_address" is suppose to be the msg.sender caller of this function however the Protocol failed to validate this before proceeding with the code implementation, only from_handler was assigned the value of msg.sender, the implication of this is that anybody can send cross chain message for another address even though they are not authorized to which can be taken advantage of to manipulate the contract functionality for an innocent user.
## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
As adjusted below Protocol should ensure "from_address" is indeed the msg.sender as noted in its comment description and the condition statement added below
```solidity
function send_cross_chain_msg(
        string memory to_chain,
        address from_address,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload
    ) external {
        nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;

        address from_handler = msg.sender;
+++        require( from_address == msg.sender, "Invalid Address")
        uint256 txid = uint256(
            keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    contract_chain_name, // from chain
                    to_chain,
                    from_address, // msg.sender address
                    from_handler, // settlement handler address
                    to_handler,
                    nonce_manager[from_address]
                )
            )
        );

        create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
            txid,
            contract_chain_name,
            to_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            payload,
            CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending
        );

        emit CrossChainMsg(
            txid,
            from_address,
            contract_chain_name,
            to_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            payload_type,
            payload
        );
    }
```

Access Control

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L327-L385
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-L244


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `receive_cross_chain_msg` uses the same logic in the [solidity version](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L170-L244) and the [cairo version](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L327-L385). The function takes a number of arguments used to receive a cross chain message and execute the handler function for this message. As the protocol utilizes off chain validators to ensure the right messages get executed, it hashes the message and verifies enough validators signed the hash. While doing so, both implementations do no include the [payload_type](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/libraries/Message.sol#L5-L20) in the hash. This mean that the hash can be changed without invalidating the signatures.

There are different payload types:
- Raw,
- BTCDeposit,
- BTCWithdraw,
- BTCStake,
- BTCUnStake,
- ERC20,
- ERC721

Right now there is only one payload type implemented (ERC20, see [cairo](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L119), [solidity](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L286-L290)). Therefor it is not possible to exploit the issue in a way to execute a different payload type, but that might be an issue with future updates. It is possible that a messaged indented to execute with type A to be frontrun and execute type B.

## Proof of Concept
N/A

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the `payload_type` to the message hash to make sure it can not be changed.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L138-L165
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L365-L396


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `receive_cross_chain_callback` is part of the [solidity handler](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L365-L396) and the [cairo handler](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L138-L165). The solidity version is called after a cross chain message was executed on the destination chain and update the transaction status based on the parameter `status` to either `CrossChainTxStatus.Settled` or `CrossChainTxStatus.Failed`. The cairo version updates the state to settled, as that implementation has no status parameter. They both complete the burn in case the mode is set to `MintBurn`.

But either implementation only handles the "happy case", that the destination transaction succeeded. **If the destination transaction can not be executed for some reason, they do not return the locked tokens to the user**. Therefor the user tokens stay locked in the handler contract or are burned forever.

## Proof of Concept
N/A

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

If the status of the transaction is `CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed` it should return the user tokens based on the `SettlementMode` by either minting new tokens or unlocking them. 


## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111-L156
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L325-L336


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
Function outputs of `send_cross_chain_msg()`  do not correlate with cairo function `receive_cross_chain_msg()` input in the `ChakraSettlement` contacts of these two versions. This could result in errors when starknet is in involved in any cross-chain message.

## Impact
Stakrtnet will be unable to receive cross-chain messages sent from or using the protocol.

## Proof Of Concept
Let's look at the output of the `send_cross_chain_msg()` in the solidity version along with the input of the `receive_cross_chain_msg()` of the cairo version.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111-L156

```solidity
    function send_cross_chain_msg(
        string memory to_chain,
        address from_address,
        uint256 to_handler,
        PayloadType payload_type,
        bytes calldata payload
    ) external {
        ...
        
        create_cross_txs[txid] = CreatedCrossChainTx(
            txid,
            contract_chain_name,
            to_chain,
            from_address,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            payload,
            CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending
        );
        ...
    }
 ```
 
 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L325-L336
 ```cairo
         fn receive_cross_chain_msg(
            ref self: ContractState,
            cross_chain_msg_id: u256,
            from_chain: felt252,
            to_chain: felt252,
            from_handler: u256,
            to_handler: ContractAddress,
            sign_type: u8,
            signatures: Array<(felt252, felt252, bool)>,
            payload: Array<u8>,
            payload_type: u8,
        ) -> bool { ... }
  ```
  Let's look at how they will match: (left side is solidity version)
  txid = cross_chain_msg_id
  contract_chain_name = from_chain
  to_chain = to_chain
  from_address (address) = from_handler (u256)
  from_handler = to_handler
  to_handler = sign_type
  payload = signatures
  CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending = payload
   ... = payload_type
   
   As can be seen above the `payload_type` will have no input and the `from_address` is a address of the msg.sender while `from_handler` is designated as a `u256`. An address in solidity is compatible with a `felt252` not `u256` in the cairo language. On top that the `to_handler` and `payload` are matched with the signature variable and array 
   This will result in the function either not operating or if it does operate it will not work as intended.
   
   ## Tools used
   Manual review
   
   ## Recommended Mitigation steps
   Ensure that the outputs from all solidity functions that will serve as inputs for cairo functions are properly matched.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L284-L314
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L167-L232


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details
In the solidity side of the contracts the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement()` function in the `ChakraSettlementHandler` contract and the `send_cross_chain_msg()` function in the `ChakraSettlement` contract make use of tracking the nonce of the user to prevent signature replay attacks by using it to create a unique `tx_id`. 

```solidity
        nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;
```

The problem here is that in the cairo side of the smart contracts, the protocol does not attempt to keep track of the user's nonce, it instead only keeps track of the transaction count.

## Impact
Users will be vulnerable to signature replay attacks on other EVM chains but not on Starknet blockchain.

#Proof Of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L284-L314
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L167-L232

```cairo
        fn send_cross_chain_msg(
            ref self: ContractState, to_chain: felt252, to_handler: u256, payload_type :u8,payload: Array<u8>,
        ) -> felt252 {
            let from_handler = get_caller_address();
            let from_chain = self.chain_name.read();
            let cross_chain_settlement_id = LegacyHash::hash(get_tx_info().unbox().transaction_hash, self.tx_count.read());
            self.created_tx.write(cross_chain_settlement_id, CreatedTx{
                tx_id:cross_chain_settlement_id,
                tx_status: CrossChainMsgStatus::PENDING,
                from_chain: from_chain,
                to_chain: to_chain,
                from_handler: from_handler,
                to_handler: to_handler
            });
            ...
```
```cairo
        fn cross_chain_erc20_settlement(ref self: ContractState, to_chain: felt252, to_handler: u256, to_token: u256, to: u256, amount: u256) -> felt252{
            ...
            
            let tx_id = LegacyHash::hash(get_tx_info().unbox().transaction_hash, self.msg_count.read());
            ...
```

By not tracking the nonce of a user and only tracking the `tx_count` or `msg_count`, when the user is performing a cross-chain message they are only protected from replay attacks in the Starknet blockchain, but they will be easily vulnerable to signature attacks on other EVM chains where their nonce has not been incremented so attackers can and will take advantage of this.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add this line in the `send_cross_chain_msg` and the `cross_chain_erc20_settlement` functions of the cairo contracts before creating the `tx_id`. Then also incorporate the nonce into the `tx_id` like you did in the solidity version of the contracts.

```diff
+ nonces.write(caller_address, value=nonce+1)
```


## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/BaseSettlementHandler.sol#L113-#L128


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The contract inherits a public initialization function from its base contract (BaseSettlementHandler) without proper access control or protection against multiple calls. This vulnerability allows an attacker to reinitialize the contract, potentially taking over ownership and modifying critical contract parameters, even after the contract has been properly set up by the legitimate owner.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/BaseSettlementHandler.sol#L113-#L128

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L82-101


The vulnerability stems from the inheritance structure and initialization pattern used in the ChakraSettlementHandler contract:

- The BaseSettlementHandler contract contains a public initialization function:

```solidity
// In BaseSettlementHandler.sol
function _Settlement_handler_init(
    address _owner,
    SettlementMode _mode,
    address _token,
    address _verifier,
    string memory _chain,
    address _settlement
) public {
    __Ownable_init(_owner);
    __UUPSUpgradeable_init();
    // ... (additional initialization)
}
```

- The ChakraSettlementHandler contract inherits from BaseSettlementHandler and introduces its own initialize function:

```solidity
// In ChakraSettlementHandler.sol
function initialize(
    address _owner,
    SettlementMode _mode,
    string memory _chain,
    address _token,
    address _codec,
    address _verifier,
    address _settlement
) public initializer {
    _Settlement_handler_init(
        _owner,
        _mode,
        _token,
        _verifier,
        _chain,
        _settlement
    );
    codec = IERC20CodecV1(_codec);
}
```

The critical issue is that while the initialize function in `ChakraSettlementHandler` is protected by the initializer modifier, the inherited _Settlement_handler_init function remains public and unprotected. This allows anyone to call this function directly on the deployed contract, potentially overwriting critical contract state and taking over ownership.

Attacker will have access to update following params 
           ```solidity
            _owner,
            _mode,
            _token,
            _verifier,
            _chain,
            _settlement
            ```
which are most important to make sure cross chain msgs/transfers works as intended.


An attacker can exploit this vulnerability using the following steps:

1. Wait for the ChakraSettlementHandler contract to be deployed and initialized by the legitimate owner.
2. Call the _Settlement_handler_init function directly on the deployed contract address:

```js
const ChakraSettlementHandler = await ethers.getContractFactory("ChakraSettlementHandler");
const deployedContract = ChakraSettlementHandler.attach("DEPLOYED_CONTRACT_ADDRESS");

await deployedContract._Settlement_handler_init(
    attackerAddress,
    1, // SettlementMode.MintBurn (could be any as per attacker wish)
    "0x1234...", // target token address
    "0x5678...", // New verifier address
    "MaliciousChain",
    "0x9ABC..." // New settlement address
);
```

3. Verify that the attacker is now the owner:

```js
const newOwner = await deployedContract.owner();
console.assert(newOwner === attackerAddress, "Ownership takeover failed");
```

## Impact
- Unauthorized Ownership Transfer: An attacker can become the owner of the contract, gaining full control over owner-only functions.
- Critical Parameter Modification: The attacker can modify essential contract parameters such as the token address, verifier, and settlement contract address.
- Disruption of Cross-Chain Operations: By changing critical addresses and parameters, the attacker can disrupt or redirect cross-chain token transfers.
- Loss of Funds: In scenarios where the contract holds or manages funds, the attacker could potentially drain or misdirect these assets.
- Loss of Trust: Such a vulnerability severely undermines trust in the protocol, potentially leading to reputational damage and loss of users.
## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Here are few recommendations, any one of them can be used:

1. Remove Public Visibility from Base Initializer:
Change the _Settlement_handler_init function in BaseSettlementHandler to internal:

```solidity
function _Settlement_handler_init(
    address _owner,
    SettlementMode _mode,
    address _token,
    address _verifier,
    string memory _chain,
    address _settlement
) internal {
    // ... (rest of the function)
}
```

2. Implement Proper Inheritance of Initializable:
Ensure both contracts correctly inherit from OpenZeppelin's Initializable:

```solidity
contract BaseSettlementHandler is Initializable {
    // ...
}

contract ChakraSettlementHandler is BaseSettlementHandler {
    // ...
}
```

3. Single Initialization Point:
Ensure that ChakraSettlementHandler's initialize function is the only entry point for initialization:

```solidity
function initialize(
    address _owner,
    SettlementMode _mode,
    string memory _chain,
    address _token,
    address _codec,
    address _verifier,
    address _settlement
) public initializer {
    _Settlement_handler_init(
        _owner,
        _mode,
        _token,
        _verifier,
        _chain,
        _settlement
    );
    codec = IERC20CodecV1(_codec);
}
```



## Assessed type

Upgradable

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111-L223
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111-L156


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The `cross_chain_erc20_settlement` function `ChakraSettlementHandler` , has inadequate input validation for the critical parameter. This oversight could lead to the processing of invalid or malicious inputs, potentially causing unexpected behaviour, contract state inconsistencies, or vulnerabilities in the cross-chain transaction process.

## Vulnerability Details
The cross_chain_erc20_settlement function in `ChakraSettlementHandler` and related functions in other contracts lack comprehensive validation for the main input parameter.

Chain Name: No validation against a list of known or allowed chains.

```solidity
function cross_chain_erc20_settlement(
    string memory to_chain,
    uint256 to_handler,
    uint256 to_token,
    uint256 to,
    uint256 amount
) external {
    // ... (token locking/burning logic)

    nonce_manager[msg.sender] += 1;

    // Create a new cross chain tx
    uint256 txid = uint256(
        keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(
                chain,
                to_chain,
                msg.sender,
                address(this),
                to_handler,
                nonce_manager[msg.sender]
            )
        )
    );

    // ... (create cross-chain transaction record)

    settlement.send_cross_chain_msg(
        to_chain,
        msg.sender,
        to_handler,
        PayloadType.ERC20,
        cross_chain_msg_bytes
    );
}
```

```solidity
function send_cross_chain_msg(
    string memory to_chain,
    address from_address,
    uint256 to_handler,
    PayloadType payload_type,
    bytes calldata payload
) external {
    // ... (create cross-chain message record)

    emit CrossChainMsg(
        txid,
        from_address,
        contract_chain_name,
        to_chain,
        from_handler,
        to_handler,
        payload_type,
        payload
    );
}
```

- No Chain ID Validation: There is no explicit validation of the to_chain parameter in either cross_chain_erc20_settlement or send_cross_chain_msg.
- Message Creation: The cross-chain message is created and an event is emitted - 
  regardless of the validity of the to_chain.
- Transaction Status: The status of the transaction is set to CrossChainTxStatus.Pending in create_cross_txs.
- Execution Continuation: The execution does not stop or revert based on the chain ID validity.


## Impact

- Message in Limbo: The cross-chain message will be created and remain in a pending state indefinitely, as there's no mechanism to validate or process messages for non-existent chains.
- Potential Token Lock: In lock/mint modes, tokens will be locked in the contract without the possibility of being unlocked on the non-existent destination chain.
- Potential Token Burn: In burn/mint modes, tokens will be burned on the source chain without the possibility of being minted on the non-existent destination chain.
- No Recovery options: There's no mechanism to detect and handle messages sent to invalid chains.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
This can be prevented by implementing a mapping for valid chains and check the input chain id against it.

```solidity

mapping(string => bool) public validChains;

function validateChain(string memory _chain) internal view {
    require(validChains[_chain], "Invalid destination chain");
}

```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

title: Front-running vulnerability in ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_callback due to unverified from_chain parameter
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L365


# Vulnerability details

## Abstract

The full lifecycle of cross-chain message 

1. User start cross-chain ERC20 transaction in [ChakraSettlementHandler.cross_chain_erc20_settlement](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L111)
This is going to generate `txid` and keep a record in `create_cross_txs[txid]`.
1. The handler from step 1 calls [ChakraSettlement.send_cross_chain_msg](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111) 
which is going to create another `txid` and keep a record in `create_cross_txs[txid]`.
1. The message is now send to destination chain and a call to [ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_callback](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L256) is expected.
1. The callback will call [ChakraSettlementHandler.receive_cross_chain_callback](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L365)
In this step the call is only processed if the status is pending, this is important to make sure that we only process any given message once.
```
require(
  [txid].status == CrossChainTxStatus.Pending,
  invalid CrossChainTxStatus"
);
```

## Attack
An attacker can watch the mempool for a valid `success` calls to `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_callback` and frontrun it with same parameters except for `from_chain`, this will result in the transaction marked as `Failed` and the success call will not be processed.

1. `ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_callback` does not validate `from_chain` input parameter.
2. It is then passed to `ChakraSettlementHandler.receive_cross_chain_callback`
if the `from_chain` is invalid this function will simply return `false` https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L374
3. Then in [ChakraSettlement.receive_cross_chain_callback](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L317) will be marked as failed `create_cross_txs[txid].status = CrossChainMsgStatus.Failed;`.
4. When the valid call is received it will [revert](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L312) because the status was changed to `Failed`.


## Impact

- All successful transaction can be marked as `failed`.
- Tokens are not burnt when the cross-chain message was successful, and depending on how this is handled by the protocol this could be a double spend.
- Watching the mempool and frontrunning is trivial so the attack can be created easily.
- Leaving the protocol in an inconsistent sate, as the transaction is marked as `Failed` in `ChakraSettlement` but it is still `Pending` in `ChakraSettlementHandler` which is [breaking invariant](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/README.md?plain=1#L108) .


## Proof of Concept

Could not make working PoC test in time, but it is possible if needed.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

- Include `from_chain` in the message signature if possible.
- In [ChakraSettlementHandler.receive_cross_chain_msg](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L375) revert instead of returning false.






## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Vulnerability details

## Abstract
The function [ChakraSettlementHandler.cross_chain_erc20_settlement](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/f61c899c22492bdf5bdcb07cdb62ea9b4cd38825/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L119) is checking supplied parameters are not zero, this is to satisfy the protocol invariant [Cross-chain ERC20 settlements can only be initiated with a valid amount (greater than 0), a valid recipient address, a valid handler address, and a valid token address.](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/README.md?plain=1#L101)

But this check is not appropriate for Starknet addresses, which are represented as felt252 (field elements) rather than uint256.

In Starknet, a valid address can be any non-zero value in the range of 0 to P-1, where P is the prime number used in the Starknet field (which is a very large number, approximately 2^251 + 17 * 2^192 + 1).


## Impact

Tokens can be sent to invalid destination. This is a high risk because it explicitly break the protocol invariant.

Manual review.

```

assert(to_token != 0 && to_token < STARKNET_PRIME, 'Invalid to token address');
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Solidity code has a critical vulnerability due to inconsistent creation of txIds between `ChakraSettlementHandler` and `ChakraSettlement` contracts.The txIds are generated by using nonce_manager storage value for both contracts. The assumption is that both contracts will produce the same txId for corresponding cross-chain transactions. However, the function `ChakraSettlement::send_cross_chain_msg` can be called by anyone, to increase spesific nonce_manager value. Due to this discrepancy, the txIds values generated by `ChakraSettlement` and `ChakraSettlementHandler` can become unsynchronized. 
This would broke the logic in `receive_cross_chain_callback` functions that shares the same txId values. Since `ChakraSettlementHandler` create_cross_txs woulnt be initialized its status would be unknown and transactions will fail.

## Proof of Concept

`ChakraSettlementHandler::cross_chain_erc20_settlement` function creates new txId using nonce_manager storage variable for a caller. Then increase msg_count and calls settlement contract.

```solidity
    function cross_chain_erc20_settlement(){
...
         nonce_manager[msg.sender] += 1;

           uint256 txid = uint256(
            keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    chain,
                    to_chain,
                    msg.sender, // from address for settlement to calculate txid
                    address(this), //  from handler for settlement to calculate
                    to_handler,
                    nonce_manager[msg.sender]
                )
            )
        );
       settlement.send_cross_chain_msg(...);

```

`ChakraSettlement::send_cross_chain_msg` function uses nonce_manager and msg.sender to create new txId. Since txId is going to be used by `receive_cross_chain_callback` functions for both contracts these two txIds must be same.  But the problem is this function can be called by anyone to increase nonce_manager without updating ChakraSettlementHandler. When this happened txId between contracts wont match.

```solidity
    function send_cross_chain_msg(){
...
        //@audit nonce can be increased by anyone
        nonce_manager[from_address] += 1;
        address from_handler = msg.sender;
        uint256 txid = uint256(
            keccak256(
                abi.encodePacked(
                    contract_chain_name, // from chain
                    to_chain,
                    from_address, // msg.sender address
                    from_handler, // settlement handler address
                    to_handler,
                    nonce_manager[from_address]
                )
            )
        );

```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L122

`ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback` uses the txId to validate and process transactions. If the txId does not match it would send a different id  to ChakraSettlementHandler.

```solidity

...
    ISettlementHandler(to_handler).receive_cross_chain_callback(
```

Inside ChakraSettlementHandler, since create_cross_txs is not initialized for received txid its status would be  `CrossChainTxStatus::Unknown` and transaction will fail.Because of this protocol callback logic is broken.
